result.text: The paper addresses the problem of efficiently producing task-specific neural architectures for previously unseen tasks, avoiding costly per-task search or poor transfers from architectures found on other tasks. Its key insight is that a task-aware architecture controller combined with meta-learned shared weights can both propose suitable architectures and quickly adapt their parameters to new tasks, because meta-weights capture a good initialization across diverse tasks and architectures. The proposed method, M-NAS, trains a controller to generate child models conditioned on task descriptors while jointly meta-learning model weights that can be fine-tuned for any sampled architecture-task pair with only a few gradient steps; at test time the controller produces a task-tailored architecture and the meta-weights are adapted rapidly to yield strong performance. Experimental results on toy regression and few-shot classification show M-NAS outperforms baselines in producing effective task-aware architectures with much greater efficiency.

The paper tackles the challenge of learning highly expressive, fine-grained human avatars—including detailed hands and facial expressions—from monocular RGB video, a setting plagued by misaligned body models and varying detail scales. Its key insight is that accurate SMPL-X alignment, adaptive control of density sensitivity across body parts, and per-pixel confidence feedback together enable more precise reconstruction and animation of subtle details when representing humans as 3D Gaussians anchored to a parametric model. Methodologically, EVA uses a plug-and-play module to correct SMPL-X-to-frame misalignment, a context-aware adaptive density control that adjusts gradient thresholds for different anatomies, and a feedback mechanism that predicts per-pixel confidence to weight Gaussian learning, producing superior quantitative and qualitative results on benchmarks, especially for hands and face.

The paper examines whether model providers can dishonestly claim to have performed machine unlearning while still retaining information about the removed data, showing that existing verification techniques are fragile. Its key insight is that current verification strategies fall into two broad types and both can be evaded by carefully designed adversarial unlearning processes that preserve utility yet hide remnants of the target data from verifiers. The authors propose two novel adversarial unlearning methods that intentionally manipulate model updates to pass verification checks while keeping predictive influence of the removed data, and they support these attacks with theoretical analysis and experiments on real-world datasets demonstrating practical success. Their results reveal fundamental vulnerabilities in present unlearning verification approaches and motivate stronger, more robust verification and defense mechanisms.

The paper addresses the difficulty of incorporating the Fréchet mean—the natural generalization of the Euclidean mean—into manifold-valued deep learning because it lacks a closed-form solution and easily computable derivatives. The key insight is that one can differentiate through the Fréchet mean on arbitrary Riemannian manifolds by deriving explicit gradient expressions and efficient solvers, and that for hyperbolic space these expressions admit a fast, accurate, and hyperparameter-free algorithm that integrates smoothly into neural network pipelines. Methodologically, the authors derive general differentiation formulas for the Fréchet mean, specialize them to hyperbolic geometry to obtain explicit gradients and a practical solver, and validate the approach by replacing aggregation in Hyperbolic GCNs—yielding state-of-the-art results on highly hyperbolic datasets—and by developing hyperbolic batch normalization that mirrors Euclidean improvements.

The paper addresses multi-source unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), where training a single shared network to learn domain-invariant features across many source domains is computationally costly and unstable, especially with min–max objectives. The key insight is to leverage prompt learning: instead of updating the whole model, learn lightweight, domain-specific prompts that capture and reduce pairwise domain gaps, then denoise and align these prompts in a compact subspace so they can generalize to new target combinations. The method, Multi-Prompt Alignment (MPA), trains an individual prompt per source–target pair with a contrastive loss to minimize domain discrepancy, auto-encodes the learned prompts to remove noise and produce a low-dimensional prompt subspace, and aligns prompts by maximizing agreement among the reconstructed prompts; this subspace also enables efficient adaptation to additional targets. Empirically, MPA is computationally efficient and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks, including an average 54.1% accuracy on DomainNet.

The paper addresses the challenge of building large pre-trained vision models specifically for medical imaging, where domain shift makes ImageNet or web-scale vision-language models suboptimal for diverse modalities and organs. Its key insight is that self-supervised pretraining on a large, heterogeneous medical-image corpus benefits from explicitly modeling pairwise image similarities and higher-order structural relationships among embeddings via a graph-matching formulation, rather than relying solely on instance-level contrastive losses. The method collects ~1.3M images across 55 public medical datasets and introduces LVM-Med, a contrastive self-supervised algorithm that integrates local and global similarity priors into a combinatorial graph-matching loss to enforce structural constraints on feature embeddings, optimized end-to-end using gradient-estimation for black-box solvers; extensive evaluation on 15 downstream tasks shows substantial gains over supervised, self-supervised, and foundation models.

The paper addresses how to perform valid, efficient statistical inference on the population-level importance of features in prediction tasks, quantified by the Shapley Population Variable Importance Measure (SPVIM), whose exact computation is exponentially expensive in the number of variables. The key insight is that one does not need to evaluate all feature coalitions to estimate the SPVIM accurately: randomly sampling only Θ(n) subsets (where n is the sample size) suffices to achieve asymptotically optimal convergence rates. The authors develop an estimator based on this randomized subset sampling, derive its asymptotic distribution to enable construction of confidence intervals and hypothesis tests, and show through theory and experiments that the procedure is computationally efficient, statistically valid, and performs well in finite samples across learning algorithms.

The paper addresses understanding long-form videos with LLM-based approaches and probes why such models perform well even when video-specific information is limited. The key insight is that much of the strong performance comes from the LLMs' world knowledge and reasoning, so augmenting them with targeted, object-centric video information—rather than raw frames—can more effectively improve accuracy. The authors propose Multimodal Video Understanding (MVU), which uses off-the-shelf vision tools to extract three object-centric modalities from videos, encodes them as natural-language descriptions, and fuses these textual modalities with the LLM to answer long-video tasks; this approach yields state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks, including robotics scenarios.

CyCLIP addresses the problem that standard contrastive image–text pretraining (e.g., CLIP) produces image and text embeddings that are not interchangeable, causing inconsistent downstream predictions despite strong overall performance. The key insight is that enforcing geometric consistency between modalities—both cross-modal (symmetrizing similarities of mismatched image–text pairs) and in-modal (aligning similarity structure within image–image and text–text pairs)—yields representations that agree across spaces and thus produce more reliable inference. The method implements this by augmenting the contrastive objective with symmetric consistency losses that explicitly regularize pairwise similarity structures in and across modalities during training, and experiments show these consistency constraints yield large improvements in zero-shot accuracy and robustness across standard benchmarks.

The paper addresses robustness in cross-modal hashing (CMH), pointing out that existing methods treat all training samples and features equally and thus are vulnerable to noisy or outlier data. The key insight is that two complementary difficulty notions—instance-level and feature-level difficulty—exist in CMH learning, and that mimicking human self-paced learning by starting from easy, reliable instances/features and progressively including harder ones can improve robustness. The proposed Dual Self-Paced Cross-Modal Hashing (DSCMH) framework assigns adaptive weights to instances and features to measure reliability, filters and downweights noisy or irrelevant data in the original space, and gradually increases those weights during training so the model learns hash codes from easy to hard; experiments on three benchmarks show superior robustness and retrieval performance over 12 state-of-the-art CMH methods.

The key insight is that, for convex losses, one can design specialized update algorithms that remove multiple points with substantially lower dependence on dimension than what follows from generic differentially private learning, yielding a separation between unlearning and privacy. Concretely, the authors develop an algorithmic framework that maintains compressed summaries and uses convexity to efficiently adjust the model after deletions, proving it can unlearn up to O(n / d^{1/4}) samples with preserved accuracy and favorable computational/storage costs, improving over the O(n / d^{1/2}) deletion guarantee implied by differential privacy.

result.text: This paper addresses how to generalize residual neural networks (ResNets) to data that lie on arbitrary Riemannian manifolds, a gap in geometric deep learning where Euclidean architectures do not directly apply to manifold-valued or hierarchically structured data. The key insight is that the residual connection can be made geometrically consistent by replacing Euclidean vector additions with manifold-aware operations (e.g., exponential and logarithm maps or parallel transport) so that skip connections respect the manifold structure and gradients propagate effectively. The method constructs Riemannian ResNet blocks that combine learned tangent-space updates with retraction (or exponential map) and appropriate transport/backpropagation rules, yielding architectures that preserve the advantages of ResNets—stable training and strong empirical performance—while being applicable to general manifolds. Empirically, the proposed Riemannian ResNets outperform prior manifold-specific networks on tasks in hyperbolic space and the manifold of symmetric positive definite matrices, showing improved metrics and training dynamics.

result.text: The paper addresses the apparent divide between contrastive and non-contrastive self-supervised learning (SSL) by asking whether their differences are fundamental or largely superficial and driven by design choices. The key insight is that contrastive criteria and covariance-based non-contrastive objectives can be algebraically related and become equivalent under certain assumptions, implying that many empirical gaps arise from hyperparameters and architecture choices rather than intrinsic methodological distinctions. To demonstrate this, the authors derive paired contrastive and non-contrastive formulations, analyze and modify popular methods (e.g., SimCLR, VICReg), propose variants that expose their connections, and empirically show that with careful hyperparameter tuning and network design SimCLR can match VICReg and that large output dimensions are not necessary for non-contrastive methods. Overall, their theoretical equivalence and experimental results suggest unifying these SOTA approaches and focusing on practical design/hyperparameter optimization to close performance gaps.

result.text: The paper addresses multi-source unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), where training a single shared network to learn domain-invariant features across many source domains is computationally costly and unstable, especially with min–max objectives. The key insight is to leverage prompt learning: instead of updating the whole model, learn lightweight, domain-specific prompts that capture and reduce pairwise domain gaps, then denoise and align these prompts in a compact subspace so they can generalize to new target combinations. The method, Multi-Prompt Alignment (MPA), trains an individual prompt per source–target pair with a contrastive loss to minimize domain discrepancy, auto-encodes the learned prompts to remove noise and produce a low-dimensional prompt subspace, and aligns prompts by maximizing agreement among the reconstructed prompts; this subspace also enables efficient adaptation to additional targets. Empirically, MPA is computationally efficient and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks, including an average 54.1% accuracy on DomainNet.

result.text: The paper addresses efficient long-video understanding with vision-language LLMs by tackling the computational bottleneck from vast numbers of video tokens. Its key insight is to encode videos streamingly into a small set of propagated, question-relevant memories rather than repeatedly processing all frames, preserving temporal context without excessive token cost. Methodologically, VideoStreaming segments videos into clips and uses Memory-Propagated Streaming Encoding to merge each clip with a distilled historical memory, then applies Adaptive Memory Selection to pick a constant number of question-related memories to feed the LLM for reasoning. This disentangled extraction-and-reasoning design reduces redundancy, enables precise temporal question answering, and yields improved accuracy and efficiency on long-video benchmarks.

The key insight is that bagging’s subsampling and majority-vote structure provides intrinsic, algorithm-agnostic resilience: if the number of poisoned training points is below a derived threshold, the ensemble’s majority vote cannot be flipped regardless of the base learner’s behavior. result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of learning useful feature representations from unlabeled 3D medical images to reduce reliance on costly expert annotations for downstream tasks. Its key insight is that popular self-supervised proxy tasks can be extended from 2D to fully volumetric 3D formulations to better capture spatial structure in medical scans, yielding richer semantic features than 2D slice-based pretraining or training from scratch. They also release an open-source library containing their 3D and 2D implementations to facilitate adoption.

args.text: We propose Intrinsic Batch Normalization and Whitening for arbitrary Riemannian manifolds, providing the missing normalization primitive for manifold-valued deep networks. Given a batch, we compute its Fréchet mean, map samples to the tangent space via the logarithm map, perform variance scaling or full whitening with learnable affine parameters in that tangent frame, and map back; gradients flow through the Fréchet mean and maps using recent differentiable formulations. We maintain running statistics by a Riemannian exponential moving average of the mean and by parallel-transporting accumulated second-moment estimates along the mean’s geodesic trajectory, enabling drop-in use in Riemannian ResNets and fully hyperbolic CNNs with improved stability and accuracy. The design admits metric-aware variants (e.g., affine-invariant for SPD) and curvature-adaptive scaling that interpolates between whitening and norm-preserving transport in highly curved regions.

result.text: The paper addresses test-time adaptation for vision-language models, aiming to improve zero-shot generalization to unlabeled target-domain images without costly backbone fine-tuning. The key insight is that leveraging self-supervised contrastive learning between prompt-conditioned representations—rather than only entropy minimization—can better exploit pre-trained model features and retain historical knowledge to stabilize adaptation. result.text: The paper addresses whether SHAP feature-attribution values can be computed efficiently for common machine learning models and data distributions. Its key insight is that computing SHAP is as hard as computing model expectations in fully-factorized distributions and is intractable even in very simple settings, implying that commonly used simplifications do not avoid worst-case hardness. Methodologically, the authors prove complexity-theoretic hardness results by reductions showing that (1) SHAP computation under product distributions reduces to computing the model's expected value (hence can be intractable for models like logistic regression), (2) SHAP is already NP/#P-hard for trivial classifiers with naive Bayes distributions, and (3) computing SHAP over the empirical distribution is #P-hard, thereby delineating precise hardness boundaries for SHAP.

result.text: DreamHuman tackles the problem of creating realistic, animatable 3D human avatars from only text descriptions, addressing limitations of prior text-to-3D systems that produce fixed, low-control, or anthropometrically inconsistent results. result.text: This paper addresses the security risk that machine unlearning—designed to remove specific data from trained models—can be abused to implant backdoors, so that the unlearned model misbehaves in the presence of a trigger. The key insight is that selectively removing particular contributed examples (or combining minor upfront poisoning with later unlearning) can shift model decision boundaries in a controlled way, enabling backdoor activation without obvious tampering of the original training set. The authors propose two attack methods: a pure-unlearning attack that achieves a backdoor solely by submitting malicious unlearning requests for a small subset of the attacker’s contributed data, and a hybrid attack that first plants a few poisoned examples with a trigger and then activates the backdoor via unlearning; both optimize attack utility while maintaining stealth. They empirically validate these attacks across multiple unlearning algorithms, model architectures, and datasets, showing that unlearning mechanisms can be exploited to reliably and covertly insert backdoors.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of existing normalizing-flow-based variational posteriors, which are confined to Euclidean space and thus poorly suited for data with hierarchical structure best captured in hyperbolic geometry. Its key insight is that normalizing flows can be generalized to hyperbolic manifolds by designing invertible, geometry-aware transformations—first by operating on the tangent bundle (Tangent Coupling, TC) and then by explicitly leveraging the hyperboloid model to produce a fully invertible wrapped transform (Wrapped Hyperboloid Coupling, WHC). The method constructs hyperbolic normalizing flows for variational inference: TC defines coupling transforms on tangent spaces with exponential/log maps to move between manifold and linear spaces, and WHC implements a learnable, efficient, and invertible mapping that respects hyperbolic metric and curvature for sampling and density evaluation. Empirically, these hyperbolic flows yield more expressive posteriors and better performance than Euclidean flows and hyperbolic VAEs on density estimation, graph reconstruction, and generative modeling of hierarchical data.

result.text: The paper studies the “modality gap,” a geometric phenomenon where different data modalities (e.g., images and text) occupy distinct, arm’s-length regions in the shared embedding space of multi-modal contrastive models like CLIP, which can hinder downstream performance and fairness. The key insight is that this gap arises from two interacting causes: (1) standard neural network initialization biases each encoder’s outputs into a narrow cone so that different encoders start separated, and (2) contrastive optimization—particularly the temperature hyperparameter—preserves or enforces a nonzero separation between modalities during training. To analyze and mitigate this, the authors combine empirical measurement and theoretical analysis of initialization-induced concentration with controlled contrastive training experiments that vary temperature and alignment forces, showing that adjusting the modality gap can substantially affect zero-shot classification accuracy and fairness outcomes.

result.text: The paper tackles synthesizing free-viewpoint video of arbitrary human performances from sparse multi-view cameras, where prior NeRF-based methods either overfit to a single person or fail to generalize to humans because of heavy occlusions and complex articulations. The key insight is to combine a parametric human body model with temporal and multi-view attention mechanisms so that tracked skeletal motion guides robust aggregation of visual evidence across time and views, enabling generalization to unseen identities and poses. Concretely, Neural Human Performer first uses a temporal transformer to fuse tracked, body-aligned features over time according to skeletal motion, then applies a multi-view transformer that cross-attends between these temporally-fused features and pixel-aligned features from each camera at each timestep to integrate multi-view observations on the fly and predict radiance fields. Experiments on ZJU-MoCap and AIST demonstrate substantial improvements over recent generalizable NeRF approaches for novel humans and poses.

result.text: This paper addresses the security risk that machine unlearning—designed to remove specific data from trained models—can be abused to implant backdoors, so that the unlearned model misbehaves in the presence of a trigger. The key insight is that selectively removing particular contributed examples (or combining minor upfront poisoning with later unlearning) can shift model decision boundaries in a controlled way, enabling backdoor activation without obvious tampering of the original training set. The authors propose two attack methods: a pure-unlearning attack that achieves a backdoor solely by submitting malicious unlearning requests for a small subset of the attacker’s contributed data, and a hybrid attack that first plants a few poisoned examples with a trigger and then activates the backdoor via unlearning; both optimize attack utility while maintaining stealth. They empirically validate these attacks across multiple unlearning algorithms, model architectures, and datasets, showing that unlearning mechanisms can be exploited to reliably and covertly insert backdoors.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of generative modeling for data concentrated on low-dimensional manifolds embedded in high-dimensional ambient spaces, where standard density estimators struggle to capture manifold geometry and yield poor inference. The key insight is to decouple learning the manifold geometry from learning a tractable probability density on that manifold, enabling models that represent both the support and the distribution on it more faithfully than ambient-space flows. The authors introduce manifold-learning flows (M-flows), which combine invertible coordinate maps (like normalizing flows) to parametrize a learned manifold with a separate density model on the manifold and a training algorithm that alternates or separates manifold and density updates rather than relying solely on maximum likelihood. args.text: We propose OT-Prompt Barycenters for continual multi-source UDA in vision–language models. We learn domain-specific prompts and compress them into a denoised latent prompt subspace, then compute a Wasserstein barycenter over source-domain feature distributions using feature banks, yielding a compositional prompt prior for unseen domains. At test time and along continual target streams, we estimate an online transport map from the barycenter to the target and update only prompts via a trust-region step that enforces gradient regularization in prompt space to avoid forgetting and swapped-prediction contrastive consistency for stable, label-free supervision. This enables fast adaptation to new domain mixtures by barycentric interpolation and reduces compute versus full-model updates, improving over prompt averaging and entropy-minimization baselines.

args.text: We propose an object-centric streaming world memory for Video-LLMs that persistently tracks slot-level entities and their relations, fusing compact latent states with natural-language summaries to preserve fine-grained, causally relevant dynamics over long videos. Each incoming clip updates the memory via mixture-of-depths routing applied per object stream, while a question-conditioned retriever selects a constant-size subgraph of relevant entities and events for the LLM to reason over. The memory is maintained as a dynamic event graph whose nodes are tracked objects with attributes and whose edges encode interactions; updates combine textual descriptions with learned latent predictors to retain non-verbal cues (e.g., velocities). Training couples unsupervised next-state prediction on object tokens with segment-level instruction tuning and retrieval supervision, aiming to improve temporal grounding, forecasting, and efficiency over frame-heavy or globally pooled baselines.

args.text: We propose Attribute-Guided Self-Paced Cross-Modal Hashing (AGSP-CMH), which builds robustness to natural distribution shifts and noisy correspondences by jointly learning from adversarial attribute perturbations and noise-aware curricula. Given interpretable attributes of image–text pairs, we synthesize paired augmentations that either preserve or flip selected attributes and solve a min–max objective that seeks worst-case attribute shifts while enforcing code invariance to allowed changes and sensitivity to flips; a dual self-paced schedule weights instances and features to gradually incorporate harder, generative perturbations. To combat spurious or erroneous pairings—especially in synthetic data—we combine complementary supervision with momentum-based correspondence correction, preventing the reinforcement of wrong matches while transferring stable semantics across modalities; we further promote hash reliability under domain shift via prototype-anchored contrastive alignment on a shared hypersphere before quantization.

result.text: We propose Intrinsic Batch Normalization and Whitening for arbitrary Riemannian manifolds, providing the missing normalization primitive for manifold-valued deep networks. Given a batch, we compute its Fréchet mean, map samples to the tangent space via the logarithm map, perform variance scaling or full whitening with learnable affine parameters in that tangent frame, and map back; gradients flow through the Fréchet mean and maps using recent differentiable formulations. We maintain running statistics by a Riemannian exponential moving average of the mean and by parallel-transporting accumulated second-moment estimates along the mean’s geodesic trajectory, enabling drop-in use in Riemannian ResNets and fully hyperbolic CNNs with improved stability and accuracy. The design admits metric-aware variants (e.g., affine-invariant for SPD) and curvature-adaptive scaling that interpolates between whitening and norm-preserving transport in highly curved regions.

The key insight is that alternating updates per modality with a reconcilement regularizer against past models lets each modality sequentially correct others’ errors, analogous to boosting, thereby balancing exploitation of uni-modal features and exploration of cross-modal interactions. Their method, ReconBoost, updates one modality at a time with a dynamically adjusted objective using a KL-based reconcilement term (preserving only the latest model per modality to avoid ensembling overfitting) and further augments this with memory consolidation and global rectification schemes; experiments on six benchmarks show improved multi-modal performance.

args.text: We propose Attribute-Adversarial Self-Paced Cross-Modal Hashing (A2-SP-CMH), which couples a dual self-paced curriculum with attribute-guided adversarial augmentation to learn robust hash codes under noisy pairs and natural shifts. An inner maximization searches along interpretable image/text attribute axes (e.g., blur/rotation and paraphrase/style) for perturbations that maximally disrupt cross-modal similarities, while self-paced instance/feature weights gradually admit harder samples and stronger perturbations over training. To avoid reinforcing wrong correspondences, a momentum teacher performs self-refining correspondence correction during learning, and a parameter-free Bi-Half balancing layer keeps each bit near half-activation before binarization. Together these components yield compact, balanced codes that are resilient to noise and attribute-level domain shifts for cross-modal retrieval.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of preserving and mining local geometric information in deep networks that operate on the Riemannian manifold of Symmetric Positive Definite (SPD) matrices, where existing SPD networks largely lack mechanisms analogous to Euclidean local convolutions. The key insight is that convolution’s role in capturing locality can be abstracted categorically and adapted to SPD manifolds, enabling principled definition of local information in Riemannian geometry rather than naively porting Euclidean filters. Based on this view the authors design a multi-scale submanifold block that constructs and processes local SPD submanifolds to extract multi-scale geometric features while respecting manifold structure and SPD constraints. Experiments across several visual tasks demonstrate that incorporating this Riemannian local mechanism improves representation quality and task performance compared to prior SPD network designs.

We propose OT-Prompt Barycenters for continual multi-source UDA in vision–language models. We learn domain-specific prompts and compress them into a denoised latent prompt subspace, then compute a Wasserstein barycenter over source-domain feature distributions using feature banks, yielding a compositional prompt prior for unseen domains. At test time and along continual target streams, we estimate an online transport map from the barycenter to the target and update only prompts via a trust-region step that enforces gradient regularization in prompt space to avoid forgetting and swapped-prediction contrastive consistency for stable, label-free supervision. This enables fast adaptation to new domain mixtures by barycentric interpolation and reduces compute versus full-model updates, improving over prompt averaging and entropy-minimization baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of quantifying valid, time-uniform uncertainty when drawing sequential samples without replacement from a finite population, which is important for deciding stopping rules and reporting estimates of a target parameter θ★. The key insight is that connections between Bayesian posteriors and martingales can be leveraged to build frequentist confidence sequences (CS) for hypergeometric parameters, and that Hoeffding- and empirical-Bernstein-style concentration can be adapted to the without-replacement setting to yield tighter time-uniform bounds. Methodologically, the authors derive a suite of CSs by first constructing martingale-based CSs via Bayesian posterior-martingale relationships for the hypergeometric model, then developing Hoeffding-type and empirical-Bernstein-type time-uniform CSs and fixed-time intervals tailored to sampling without replacement, which provably improve on prior bounds.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of learning useful representations from unlabeled medical data when available samples span both 2D images and 3D volumes, a setting where existing self-supervised methods are typically limited to one modality and cannot exploit mixed datasets or transfer across dimensionalities. Its key insight is to jointly learn 2D and 3D representations by combining a 2D contrastive clustering objective on images/slices with a novel 3D clustering-agreement objective and masked-embedding prediction that aggregates slice-wise embeddings into holistic volume features via deformable self-attention in a Transformer. Methodologically, the approach extracts vectored embeddings from individual slices, assembles them into long-range-aware volume representations with deformable attention, applies 2D contrastive clustering on slices and a 3D agreement/clustering loss plus masked prediction on volume embeddings to enforce consistency, and pretrains networks that transfer to diverse downstream tasks. Experiments on brain, lung, heart, and chest X-ray benchmarks show this joint 2D–3D SSL outperforms plain 2D clustering methods and many contemporary 2D and 3D self-supervised approaches.

args.text: Current sampling-based estimators of Shapley population variable importance and interactions require a preset budget and provide only fixed-time guarantees, lacking anytime-valid uncertainty and principled stopping. We propose Anytime-SHAP-CS, a sequential design that adaptively samples coalitions and builds time-uniform confidence sequences for feature- and interaction-level attributions via martingale-based empirical-Bernstein bounds for bounded coalition contributions. By combining the O(n)-subset randomized estimation for SPVIM with unified interaction sampling (e.g., SHAP-IQ), our method allocates samples to the most uncertain attributions and stops once all intervals meet a target width, while maintaining simultaneous coverage across all targets. This enables rigorous online inference, multiple-hypothesis testing, and substantial computational savings in streaming or budgeted settings.

result.text: The paper tackles unsupervised learning of object-centric visual dynamics from videos, aiming to disentangle objects and predict their future states for tasks like long-term video synthesis, VQA, and planning. The key insight is that operating a powerful autoregressive Transformer over learned slot-based object representations lets the model explicitly reason about spatio-temporal relationships between objects, yielding more accurate and coherent future states than pixel- or scene-level predictors. The method—SlotFormer—first extracts object-centric slots from video frames with an existing slot-based perception module, then feeds sequences of these slots into a Transformer dynamics model to autoregressively predict future slot trajectories and decode them into pixels; this unsupervised dynamics model both improves long-horizon visual generation and transfers to downstream supervised tasks and model-based planning without object labels.

args.text: We propose Predictive Object Memory (POM), a long-video VLM that maintains a compact, question-conditioned belief over objects and relations to enable precise temporal reasoning with few visual tokens. POM extracts object slots and learns a lightweight dynamics prior to predict state transitions between sparse observations; only change-points are surfaced to the LLM as natural-language updates, while a streaming controller decides when to observe next. The dynamics prior operates over object-centric tokens and is distilled into text via object-centric descriptions, and the controller is optimized with segment-level instruction supervision and counterfactual rollouts to request observations when uncertainty or relevance spikes. By replacing dense frame tokens with predictive, object-centric event updates, POM improves moment localization and QA accuracy in long, partially observable streams at a fraction of the compute.

result.text: Current sampling-based estimators of Shapley population variable importance and interactions require a preset budget and provide only fixed-time guarantees, lacking anytime-valid uncertainty and principled stopping. We propose Anytime-SHAP-CS, a sequential design that adaptively samples coalitions and builds time-uniform confidence sequences for feature- and interaction-level attributions via martingale-based empirical-Bernstein bounds for bounded coalition contributions. By combining the O(n)-subset randomized estimation for SPVIM with unified interaction sampling (e.g., SHAP-IQ), our method allocates samples to the most uncertain attributions and stops once all intervals meet a target width, while maintaining simultaneous coverage across all targets. This enables rigorous online inference, multiple-hypothesis testing, and substantial computational savings in streaming or budgeted settings.

result.text: HumanSplat addresses the challenge of generating high-fidelity, generalizable 3D human reconstructions from a single image without requiring dense multi-view captures or per-instance optimization. The key insight is to predict 3D Gaussian splatting properties directly from one image by combining learned geometric priors about human structure with powerful multi-view and latent modeling, allowing the system to infer consistent shapes, colors, and view-dependent appearance for novel-view synthesis. The method integrates a 2D multi-view diffusion model that hallucinates coherent multi-view image evidence with a latent reconstruction transformer that fuses semantic features and human structure priors into 3D Gaussian parameters, and it is trained with a hierarchical loss that leverages human semantic cues to better constrain multi-view consistency and texture detail. Experiments on benchmarks and in-the-wild images show HumanSplat produces more photorealistic novel views than prior single-image and generalizable human reconstruction approaches.

result.text: COPT addresses the problem of defining a meaningful, unsupervised distance between graphs that captures both node-level correspondences and global structural (spectral) properties for tasks like graph comparison and sketching. result.text: We propose Uncertainty Interaction Shapley (UIS), extending predictive-uncertainty Shapley attributions to higher-order interactions by formulating the entropy-based characteristic function within the weighted least squares (WLS) framework that underlies Shapley interaction indices, yielding a unified objective and estimator. Concretely, we define k-order coefficients that jointly reconstruct conditional-entropy games via optimal WLS and estimate them with a single representation-driven sampler in the spirit of SHAP-IQ, sharing lower-order terms for variance reduction. To compute entropy terms robustly and efficiently, we plug in RKHS conditional-embedding estimators of conditional entropies/mutual informations and derive CLT-style asymptotics and valid confidence intervals by adapting randomized-coalition inference machinery from SPVIM to this WLS setting. The result is a scalable, statistically grounded method to explain which feature interactions drive model uncertainty, enabling targeted acquisition of synergistic features and covariate-shift diagnosis.

result.text: The paper examines whether model providers can dishonestly claim to have performed machine unlearning while still retaining information about the removed data, showing that existing verification techniques are fragile. Its key insight is that current verification strategies fall into two broad types and both can be evaded by carefully designed adversarial unlearning processes that preserve utility yet hide remnants of the target data from verifiers. The authors propose two novel adversarial unlearning methods that intentionally manipulate model updates to pass verification checks while keeping predictive influence of the removed data, and they support these attacks with theoretical analysis and experiments on real-world datasets demonstrating practical success. Their results reveal fundamental vulnerabilities in present unlearning verification approaches and motivate stronger, more robust verification and defense mechanisms.

result.text: We propose Predictive Object Memory (POM), a long-video VLM that maintains a compact, question-conditioned belief over objects and relations to enable precise temporal reasoning with few visual tokens. POM extracts object slots and learns a lightweight dynamics prior to predict state transitions between sparse observations; only change-points are surfaced to the LLM as natural-language updates, while a streaming controller decides when to observe next. The dynamics prior operates over object-centric tokens and is distilled into text via object-centric descriptions, and the controller is optimized with segment-level instruction supervision and counterfactual rollouts to request observations when uncertainty or relevance spikes. By replacing dense frame tokens with predictive, object-centric event updates, POM improves moment localization and QA accuracy in long, partially observable streams at a fraction of the compute.

args.text: We propose Partial-OT CLIP: augment contrastive image–text pretraining with a mini-batch partial optimal transport regularizer that softly aligns only the most reliable cross-modal pairs beyond the labeled matches, encouraging overlap of image and text embedding subspaces while avoiding spurious correspondences. result.text: The paper addresses how to learn generative models over neural network weights from a model zoo so one can sample new, high-performing networks for tasks like initialization, ensembling and transfer learning. The key insight is that a learned hyper-representation (an autoencoder latent space of whole-model weights) can be turned into a generative model if training stabilizes across layers and sampling follows the geometry of that latent space. The authors introduce layer-wise loss normalization during hyper-autoencoder training to balance contributions from different layers and propose several latent-space sampling strategies (e.g., around latent clusters or along manifold directions) to produce diverse candidate weights. args.text: ZK-Unlearn: a publicly verifiable machine unlearning protocol that attaches a zero-knowledge proof to every "forgotten" model release certifying it equals retraining on the original committed dataset with the requested records removed. Providers pre-commit to dataset Merkle roots, initialization, and SGD randomness; upon a deletion they release the updated weights plus a succinct proof that running (DP-)SGD on the committed data minus the specified leaves yields exactly those weights, without revealing anything about the data or which records were deleted. The protocol uses proof-friendly training traces (e.g., quantized/low-precision gradients and layerwise chunking) and batched polynomial commitments to keep proving costs practical, and composes with DP to mitigate update-leakage and remain sound under adaptively chosen deletions. This closes the gap exploited by current unlearning verifiers by making correctness auditable by anyone without retraining or trusting the provider.

result.text: The paper addresses the difficulty of incorporating the Fréchet mean—the natural generalization of the Euclidean mean—into manifold-valued deep learning because it lacks a closed-form solution and easily computable derivatives. Methodologically, the authors derive general differentiation formulas for the Fréchet mean, specialize them to hyperbolic geometry to obtain explicit gradients and a practical solver, and validate the approach by replacing aggregation in Hyperbolic GCNs—yielding state-of-the-art results on highly hyperbolic datasets—and by developing hyperbolic batch normalization that mirrors Euclidean improvements.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of domain generalization for vision models when collecting images for every possible deployment domain is impractical, asking whether simply describing both seen and unseen domains in language can improve robustness. result.text: The paper addresses how to perform valid, efficient statistical inference on the population-level importance of features in prediction tasks, quantified by the Shapley Population Variable Importance Measure (SPVIM), whose exact computation is exponentially expensive in the number of variables. The key insight is that one does not need to evaluate all feature coalitions to estimate the SPVIM accurately: randomly sampling only Θ(n) subsets (where n is the sample size) suffices to achieve asymptotically optimal convergence rates. The authors develop an estimator based on this randomized subset sampling, derive its asymptotic distribution to enable construction of confidence intervals and hypothesis tests, and show through theory and experiments that the procedure is computationally efficient, statistically valid, and performs well in finite samples across learning algorithms.

result.text: We propose Predictive Object Memory (POM), a long-video VLM that maintains a compact, question-conditioned belief over objects and relations to enable precise temporal reasoning with few visual tokens. POM extracts object slots and learns a lightweight dynamics prior to predict state transitions between sparse observations; only change-points are surfaced to the LLM as natural-language updates, while a streaming controller decides when to observe next. The dynamics prior operates over object-centric tokens and is distilled into text via object-centric descriptions, and the controller is optimized with segment-level instruction supervision and counterfactual rollouts to request observations when uncertainty or relevance spikes. By replacing dense frame tokens with predictive, object-centric event updates, POM improves moment localization and QA accuracy in long, partially observable streams at a fraction of the compute.

args.text: We propose pose-conditioned State-Space Gaussians for streaming monocular-to-avatar capture: a canonical Gaussian field plus a compact state-space updater that predicts per-part Gaussian position/scale/opacity and view-dependent color residuals conditioned on SMPL-X pose. Per-part adaptive density and per-pixel confidence preserve fine hands/face detail, while a pose-aligned temporal fusion module and a diffusion-guided multi-view hallucinator supervise occlusions and accelerate convergence. An explicit canonical-and-deformation factorization enables semantically consistent pose/expression edits, and the SSM propagates appearance and geometry across time for temporally stable, real-time rendering. Compared to prior human Gaussian or NeRF pipelines, this yields robust, editable avatars under fast motion with strong detail and 60+ FPS rendering.

result.text: ZK-Unlearn: a publicly verifiable machine unlearning protocol that attaches a zero-knowledge proof to every "forgotten" model release certifying it equals retraining on the original committed dataset with the requested records removed. Providers pre-commit to dataset Merkle roots, initialization, and SGD randomness; upon a deletion they release the updated weights plus a succinct proof that running (DP-)SGD on the committed data minus the specified leaves yields exactly those weights, without revealing anything about the data or which records were deleted. The protocol uses proof-friendly training traces (e.g., quantized/low-precision gradients and layerwise chunking) and batched polynomial commitments to keep proving costs practical, and composes with DP to mitigate update-leakage and remain sound under adaptively chosen deletions. This closes the gap exploited by current unlearning verifiers by making correctness auditable by anyone without retraining or trusting the provider.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of learning flexible probability distributions on data that lie on Riemannian manifolds (e.g., spheres, tori, hyperbolic spaces), where standard normalizing flows—built for Euclidean (flat) spaces—are misspecified and perform poorly. Its key insight is that continuous normalizing flows can be generalized to Riemannian manifolds by defining the flow as the solution of an ODE whose vector field respects the manifold geometry, allowing exact transformation of densities via the manifold-aware continuity equation rather than flat-space change-of-variable formulas. The method parameterizes a time-dependent tangent-vector field on the manifold, integrates the induced ODE to push a base density along manifold-respecting trajectories, and computes log-density changes using the Riemannian divergence (trace of the covariant derivative) to train the model; experiments show substantial improvements over Euclidean and projected-flow baselines on synthetic and real datasets.

result.text: The paper addresses multi-source unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), where training a single shared network to learn domain-invariant features across many source domains is computationally costly and unstable, especially with min–max objectives. The key insight is to leverage prompt learning: instead of updating the whole model, learn lightweight, domain-specific prompts that capture and reduce pairwise domain gaps, then denoise and align these prompts in a compact subspace so they can generalize to new target combinations. The method, Multi-Prompt Alignment (MPA), trains an individual prompt per source–target pair with a contrastive loss to minimize domain discrepancy, auto-encodes the learned prompts to remove noise and produce a low-dimensional prompt subspace, and aligns prompts by maximizing agreement among the reconstructed prompts; this subspace also enables efficient adaptation to additional targets. Empirically, MPA is computationally efficient and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks, including an average 54.1% accuracy on DomainNet.

args.text: We propose TriMed-Struct: a unified pretraining framework that jointly learns from 2D slices, 3D volumes, and accompanying radiology reports by coupling local masked modeling with global graph-structured constraints across patients and modalities. Specifically, we introduce cross-modality masked volume modeling that conditions on observed modalities and an explicit modality mask to reconstruct masked-out modality tokens at both slice and volume levels, while enforcing slice–volume clustering agreement and masked-embedding prediction for robust 2D–3D consistency. A graph-matching structural loss aligns patient-level embeddings aggregated over modalities and text (via masked report completion) to preserve global pathology relationships, and an auxiliary intermediate-layer alignment objective ties the 2D and 3D branches to learn reusable mid-level features. We hypothesize this tri-modal structural SSL substantially improves label efficiency for segmentation and cross-modality synthesis, outperforming image-only or text-only pretraining across diverse medical benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of efficiently and generally estimating any-order Shapley interaction indices—extensions of Shapley values that quantify feature interactions—when multiple competing definitions exist and each requires bespoke approximation methods. The key insight is that all cardinal interaction indices (those satisfying linearity, symmetry and dummy axioms) admit a unified representation that enables a single sampling-based estimator with provable approximation quality and variance estimates. The authors introduce SHAP-IQ, a novel representation-driven sampler that generalizes and simplifies existing estimators (recovering an unbiased KernelSHAP form for the Shapley value) and provides theoretical error bounds and variance estimates. They demonstrate SHAP-IQ’s computational efficiency and effectiveness on language and image classification tasks and high-dimensional synthetic models.

result.text: The paper addresses efficient long-video understanding with vision-language LLMs by tackling the computational bottleneck from vast numbers of video tokens. Its key insight is to encode videos streamingly into a small set of propagated, question-relevant memories rather than repeatedly processing all frames, preserving temporal context without excessive token cost. Methodologically, VideoStreaming segments videos into clips and uses Memory-Propagated Streaming Encoding to merge each clip with a distilled historical memory, then applies Adaptive Memory Selection to pick a constant number of question-related memories to feed the LLM for reasoning. This disentangled extraction-and-reasoning design reduces redundancy, enables precise temporal question answering, and yields improved accuracy and efficiency on long-video benchmarks.

result.text: We propose Partial-OT CLIP: augment contrastive image–text pretraining with a mini-batch partial optimal transport regularizer that softly aligns only the most reliable cross-modal pairs beyond the labeled matches, encouraging overlap of image and text embedding subspaces while avoiding spurious correspondences. On each batch, we compute a partial OT plan between image and text embeddings under cosine distance, transport only an α-fraction of mass to nearest neighbors, and impose symmetric consistency on these soft matches while training with geodesic-mixup hard negatives on the residual mass; simultaneously, we adapt the InfoNCE temperature by monitoring an online estimate of the modality-cone separation. This combines geometric consistency and hard-negative shaping with robust partial matching, directly targeting the initialization- and temperature-driven modality gap to yield more interchangeable embeddings and improved zero-shot and retrieval robustness.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of image-text matching degraded by noisy correspondences in training data, which cause models to overfit erroneous pairings and hurt retrieval performance. Its key insight is that combining an active/complementary supervision strategy with a self-refining, momentum-based correction process can both reduce the risk of reinforcing wrong labels and progressively recover true pairings. Concretely, the authors introduce Cross-modal Robust Complementary Learning (CRCL) composed of an Active Complementary Loss (ACL) that provides complementary and less error-prone supervision to deter memorization of noise, and a Self-refining Correspondence Correction (SCC) that iteratively refines pair corrections using momentum aggregation to expand the correction context and prevent error accumulation; experiments on Flickr30K, MS-COCO and CC152K show improved robustness to synthetic and real-world noisy correspondences.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of learning flexible, tractable meta-distributions over functions for tasks like regression and Bayesian inference, improving on limitations of existing neural process methods. The key insight is to combine denoising diffusion generative modeling with architectural inductive biases for stochastic processes—specifically exchangeability—so the model directly learns to sample finite marginals of function-valued distributions. The proposed method, Neural Diffusion Processes (NDPs), uses a diffusion-based generation scheme together with a custom attention block that enforces permutation invariance and other process properties, training the model to reverse a noising process on function values conditioned on inputs. Empirically, NDPs closely approximate true Bayesian posteriors (e.g., emulating Gaussian processes), outperform neural processes, and support tasks like implicit hyperparameter marginalization, non-Gaussian posterior prediction, and global optimization.

args.text: We propose Canonical Diffusion-Perceptual Gaussian Avatars: from monocular video, learn a SMPL-X–anchored canonical 3D Gaussian field and a deformation network that maps posed points back to canonical space for rendering. To overcome occlusions and sparse views, a lightweight part-aware multi-view diffusion prior hallucinates auxiliary, pose-aligned novel views per frame and produces uncertainty maps that gate Gaussian updates. Training blends photometric terms with full-image perceptual supervision to enforce global texture and view-dependent consistency while an EVA-style per-pixel confidence modulates gradients on fine parts like hands and face. The result is a fast-to-render, fully editable avatar that better preserves fine details and generalizes across poses compared to prior single-view Gaussian or canonical-only approaches.

result.text: The paper tackles the limitation of current vision-language-action models that operate on 2D inputs and directly map perception to actions without an explicit model of 3D dynamics for planning. Its key insight is that embedding a generative 3D world model into an embodied foundation model—by combining 3D perception, reasoning, and action with generative prediction of future scenes—enables more robust reasoning and action planning. Concretely, 3D-VLA builds a 3D-aware large language model augmented with interaction tokens and aligned embodied diffusion models that generate goal images and point clouds, and it is trained on a large-scale 3D instruction dataset assembled from existing robotics data to learn the relations between actions and environment dynamics. Experiments on held-in datasets show that this approach improves multimodal generation, reasoning, and planning in embodied environments, demonstrating the utility of generative 3D world models for real-world tasks.

The paper addresses unsupervised domain adaptation under Generalized Target Shift (GeTarS), where both class-conditional distributions and label proportions differ between source and target domains, a setting poorly handled by existing methods that force representation invariance. The key insight is to avoid insisting on invariant features and instead learn an explicit optimal transport map in a pretrained representation space that directly maps source representations to target ones, which can simultaneously align conditional distributions and recover target label proportions. Methodologically, they parameterize the optimal transport map as a neural network trained to push source representations to match the target distribution while preserving class-conditional structure, and provide theoretical guarantees of uniqueness, conditional matching, proportion recovery, and controlled target risk under mild assumptions. Empirically, this flexible, scalable approach outperforms prior GeTarS methods across multiple datasets.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of extending Shapley-value explanations to reliably quantify higher-order feature interactions (Shapley Interaction Index, SII) by showing whether and how SII can be derived as the optimum of a weighted least squares (WLS) approximation, closing a long-standing theoretical gap that previously motivated alternative interaction indices. The key insight is that SII together with lower-order k-Shapley values form the coefficients of an optimal WLS reconstruction of a game, analogous to how the Shapley value minimizes a specific WLS for single-feature attributions; the authors prove this equivalence for the Shapley value and pairwise interactions and present empirically supported conjectures for higher orders. Methodologically, they derive the appropriate weighting scheme and closed-form characterization, then implement KernelSHAP-IQ—a direct extension of KernelSHAP that solves the resulting WLS to estimate interaction attributions—and validate it empirically to achieve state-of-the-art performance for detecting and quantifying feature interactions.

The key insight is that training a Video-LLM on large-scale, segment-level instruction data enables fine-grained temporal reasoning and grounding rather than just global video understanding. To realize this, the authors build an automatic data-generation engine to create Moment-10M, a massive dataset of videos paired with segment-level instructions, and train Momentor on this data so it can reason about, locate, and answer questions about precise moments in videos; zero-shot evaluations show strong performance on temporally grounded comprehension and localization tasks.

result.text: The paper tackles unsupervised domain adaptive hashing for image retrieval, where transferring semantic structure from a labelled source to an unlabelled target while producing compact hash codes is challenging because prior adaptations either naively reuse domain-adaptation tactics or align features in Hamming space with limited semantic fidelity. The key insight is to learn a domain-shared unit hypersphere of prototype-anchored, contrastively trained features that are both uniformly distributed and resistant to category conflicts, then map those continuous features to a Hamming hypersphere so that semantic relations are preserved during quantization. Methodologically, Comparative Prototype Hashing (CPH) constructs class prototypes and performs prototype contrastive learning across domains to eliminate domain gaps in the shared hypersphere, supervises hashing with dual-domain similarity information, and finally maps features to binary codes on a Hamming hypersphere; this yields substantially improved cross-domain and single-domain retrieval performance on benchmarks like Office-Home and Office-31.

result.text: The paper tackles the inefficiency and uncertainty in transfer learning when selecting pretrained models for new tasks, especially the high cost and limited scalability of training or fine-tuning many models and the poor transfer when source and target data differ. The key insight is to learn a generative distribution over neural network parameters using a latent diffusion model conditioned on target-data representations, enabling direct generation of high-quality weights that generalize across seen and unseen tasks without access to original training data. The method, D2NWG, adapts generative hyper-representation learning to model weight distributions of networks pretrained on diverse datasets, trains a conditional latent diffusion process to map dataset-conditioned latents to network parameters, and then samples task-specific weights for arbitrary architectures (including LLMs) to produce performant models without further fine-tuning. Extensive experiments show this approach outperforms meta-learning baselines and pretrained models across model sizes, demonstrating a scalable way to generate task-adapted parameters for transfer learning.

result.text: DELIFFAS tackles the challenge of synthesizing controllable, photorealistic human avatars that are both high-quality and fast to render. The key insight is to model a person’s appearance as a deformable surface light field attached to a controllable mesh, enabling a compact, image-space representation that can be evaluated quickly while still capturing view-dependent effects. Methodologically, the authors represent the light field with a two-surface parameterization that deforms with the underlying mesh and train it with full-image perceptual supervision (rather than only per-pixel/patch losses), yielding fast inference and state-of-the-art synthesis quality.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of machine unlearning: given a model trained on dataset S, how to efficiently remove the influence of one or more training points later while retaining provable generalization on future data. The key insight is that, for convex losses, one can design specialized update algorithms that remove multiple points with substantially lower dependence on dimension than what follows from generic differentially private learning, yielding a separation between unlearning and privacy. Concretely, the authors develop an algorithmic framework that maintains compressed summaries and uses convexity to efficiently adjust the model after deletions, proving it can unlearn up to O(n / d^{1/4}) samples with preserved accuracy and favorable computational/storage costs, improving over the O(n / d^{1/2}) deletion guarantee implied by differential privacy.

result.text: We propose OT-Prompt Barycenters for continual multi-source UDA in vision–language models. We learn domain-specific prompts and compress them into a denoised latent prompt subspace, then compute a Wasserstein barycenter over source-domain feature distributions using feature banks, yielding a compositional prompt prior for unseen domains. At test time and along continual target streams, we estimate an online transport map from the barycenter to the target and update only prompts via a trust-region step that enforces gradient regularization in prompt space to avoid forgetting and swapped-prediction contrastive consistency for stable, label-free supervision. This enables fast adaptation to new domain mixtures by barycentric interpolation and reduces compute versus full-model updates, improving over prompt averaging and entropy-minimization baselines.

result.text: We propose TriMed-Struct: a unified pretraining framework that jointly learns from 2D slices, 3D volumes, and accompanying radiology reports by coupling local masked modeling with global graph-structured constraints across patients and modalities. Specifically, we introduce cross-modality masked volume modeling that conditions on observed modalities and an explicit modality mask to reconstruct masked-out modality tokens at both slice and volume levels, while enforcing slice–volume clustering agreement and masked-embedding prediction for robust 2D–3D consistency. A graph-matching structural loss aligns patient-level embeddings aggregated over modalities and text (via masked report completion) to preserve global pathology relationships, and an auxiliary intermediate-layer alignment objective ties the 2D and 3D branches to learn reusable mid-level features. We hypothesize this tri-modal structural SSL substantially improves label efficiency for segmentation and cross-modality synthesis, outperforming image-only or text-only pretraining across diverse medical benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses learning cross-modal tasks when paired multi-modal data is scarce by studying why pre-trained multi-modal contrastive spaces still exhibit a modality gap that prevents embeddings from different modalities being truly interchangeable. The key insight is a theoretical characterization of the contrastive embedding geometry that reveals persistent modality-specific structure, and that explicitly connecting modalities, collapsing intra-modality variance, and introducing controlled corruption can align those spaces to improve interchangeability. The authors propose C^3 (Connect, Collapse, Corrupt): connect by synthesizing or mapping anchors across modalities to create alignment pairs, collapse by reducing within-modality dispersion so representations occupy a shared subspace, and corrupt by applying noise/augmentation to encourage robustness and overlap between modalities. Its key insight is that leveraging intra-modal manifold structure can correct noisy cross-modal similarities: traversing heterogeneous manifolds within each modality reveals more reliable relationships than relying solely on a learned common space. result.text: The paper tackles the problem of compressing large numbers of Gaussians and their attributes in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for novel view synthesis, where existing methods compress each Gaussian independently and ignore spatial interactions. The key insight is to apply an anchor-level autoregressive context model—grouping anchors into multiple levels so that uncoded anchors can be predicted from already coded anchors in coarser levels—to exploit inter-anchor dependencies and improve entropy modeling. Methodologically, they implement this multilevel context prediction and additionally introduce a low-dimensional quantized feature as a hyperprior per anchor to efficiently code levels with few or no prior anchors, enabling more effective entropy coding. The approach achieves over 100× size reduction versus vanilla 3DGS and ~15× versus recent Scaffold-GS while maintaining comparable or better rendering quality.

The paper addresses the problem of building flexible, general-purpose normalizing flows that respect non‑Euclidean data geometry without requiring handcrafted, manifold‑specific layers. Its key insight is that Neural ODEs can be generalized to arbitrary manifolds using only local geometric information, enabling continuous-time flows whose dynamics remain on the manifold and whose probability densities can be tracked via a continuous change-of-variables formula. The authors introduce Neural Manifold ODEs and use them to construct Manifold Continuous Normalizing Flows (MCNFs), which integrate vector fields defined in local charts (or via embeddings) to transport probability mass while computing log-densities through an ODE for the instantaneous change of variables. Empirically, MCNFs are simple to apply across different manifolds and produce improved density estimation and downstream task performance compared with prior manifold-specific flow designs.

Its key insight is that decomposing videos into object-centric tokens—treating objects as the “words” of a scene—yields a compact, semantically meaningful representation that lets a transformer model learn complex spatio-temporal interactions unsupervised. The proposed Object-Centric Video Transformer (OCVT) first unsupervisedly segments frames into object slots and encodes those slots as tokens, then trains a generative transformer over sequences of object tokens to predict future object states and render frames, achieving much lower memory use than pixel-based approaches and enabling training on sequences up to 70 frames while improving generation quality and downstream video reasoning (e.g., state-of-the-art on CATER).

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of efficiently producing task-specific neural architectures for previously unseen tasks, avoiding costly per-task search or poor transfers from architectures found on other tasks. Its key insight is that a task-aware architecture controller combined with meta-learned shared weights can both propose suitable architectures and quickly adapt their parameters to new tasks, because meta-weights capture a good initialization across diverse tasks and architectures. The proposed method, M-NAS, trains a controller to generate child models conditioned on task descriptors while jointly meta-learning model weights that can be fine-tuned for any sampled architecture-task pair with only a few gradient steps; at test time the controller produces a task-tailored architecture and the meta-weights are adapted rapidly to yield strong performance. Experimental results on toy regression and few-shot classification show M-NAS outperforms baselines in producing effective task-aware architectures with much greater efficiency.

The paper addresses the challenge of diffusion-based 3D human generation, where existing approaches struggle with the heavy computational cost of volumetric representations and the articulated topology of human bodies. Its key insight is to run the denoising diffusion process directly on a set of volumetric primitives—small, parameterized volumes that jointly encode radiance and kinematic information—thereby combining the expressiveness of volumetric models with the efficiency of primitive-based rendering. The method, PrimDiffusion, learns a compact diffusion model over primitive parameters (shape, color, pose-related transforms) and decodes them with a decoder-free rendering pipeline for efficient novel-view and novel-pose synthesis; this yields a flexible 3D prior that supports real-time high-resolution rendering after denoising and enables training-free conditional tasks like texture transfer and 3D inpainting, outperforming prior GAN-based and other baselines.

result.text: This paper addresses the security risk that machine unlearning—designed to remove specific data from trained models—can be abused to implant backdoors, so that the unlearned model misbehaves in the presence of a trigger. The key insight is that selectively removing particular contributed examples (or combining minor upfront poisoning with later unlearning) can shift model decision boundaries in a controlled way, enabling backdoor activation without obvious tampering of the original training set. The authors propose two attack methods: a pure-unlearning attack that achieves a backdoor solely by submitting malicious unlearning requests for a small subset of the attacker’s contributed data, and a hybrid attack that first plants a few poisoned examples with a trigger and then activates the backdoor via unlearning; both optimize attack utility while maintaining stealth. They empirically validate these attacks across multiple unlearning algorithms, model architectures, and datasets, showing that unlearning mechanisms can be exploited to reliably and covertly insert backdoors.

args.text: We propose Conformal Metric Continuous Normalizing Flows (CM-CNFs), which learn a scalar conformal factor over the ambient space to define a Riemannian metric that warps volumes around the data, and evolve a continuous-time flow whose dynamics and log-density updates are computed with respect to this learned geometry. Because conformal metrics admit closed-form adjustments to divergence and volume elements relative to Euclidean space, we can track exact likelihoods w.r.t. Lebesgue measure while jointly learning geometry (the conformal factor) and transport (the vector field) in continuous time. result.text: The paper addresses test-time domain adaptation where a model trained on source domains must adapt to an unseen target domain using a few unlabeled images, noting that naively updating whole networks mixes label and domain knowledge and causes interference. Its key insight is that domain information can be effectively learned by manipulating only batch normalization (BN) parameters—specifically the two affine parameters—while keeping source BN statistics fixed, which stabilizes adaptation from few samples, and that a label-independent self-supervised auxiliary branch can provide complementary domain signals. Methodologically, they update only BN affine parameters during adaptation, add an auxiliary SSL branch to extract domain knowledge, and employ a bi-level meta-learning optimization to align the auxiliary and main objectives; the auxiliary branch is discarded at inference so computational cost stays unchanged, and experiments on five WILDS datasets show improved performance over prior methods.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of learning compact, task-agnostic representations of whole neural network weight spaces that scale to larger models and multiple downstream tasks, overcoming prior methods that were either size-limited or task-specific. The key insight is to extend hyper-representations by processing neural network weights sequentially as subsets (tokens), enabling a scalable embedding mechanism that captures global model information through layer-wise embeddings and supports generation of new network weights. The proposed method, SANE, tokenizes networks into sequential weight subsets, feeds these tokens into a learned encoder to produce a set representation and layer-wise embeddings, and uses this sequential representation both for downstream tasks (e.g., initialization for new tasks) and for autoregressive generation of unseen models. Empirically, SANE matches or outperforms prior weight-representation approaches on benchmarks, particularly improving transfer and initialization for larger architectures like ResNets.

result.text: The paper tackles the limited accuracy of self-supervised multi-frame (MVS-style) depth estimation from monocular video, which struggles with texture-less regions, non-Lambertian surfaces, moving objects, and unknown camera motion. The key insight is to treat monocular depth predictions as a geometric prior to guide and constrain the multi-view cost volume, and to use predicted camera velocity to adaptively adjust depth candidates, while learning uncertainty to fuse monocular and MVS cues. The method, called MOVEDepth, constructs an MVS cost volume centered on monocular depth, refines candidate depths under velocity guidance, and combines monocular and multi-view depths via uncertainty-aware fusion, yielding substantially improved and more robust self-supervised depth estimates across KITTI and DDAD.

result.text: We propose Intrinsic Batch Normalization and Whitening for arbitrary Riemannian manifolds, providing the missing normalization primitive for manifold-valued deep networks. Given a batch, we compute its Fréchet mean, map samples to the tangent space via the logarithm map, perform variance scaling or full whitening with learnable affine parameters in that tangent frame, and map back; gradients flow through the Fréchet mean and maps using recent differentiable formulations. We maintain running statistics by a Riemannian exponential moving average of the mean and by parallel-transporting accumulated second-moment estimates along the mean’s geodesic trajectory, enabling drop-in use in Riemannian ResNets and fully hyperbolic CNNs with improved stability and accuracy. The design admits metric-aware variants (e.g., affine-invariant for SPD) and curvature-adaptive scaling that interpolates between whitening and norm-preserving transport in highly curved regions.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of training accurate medical image segmentation models when labeled volumetric data are scarce by improving self-supervised pretraining for semi-supervised segmentation. The key insight is that contrastive learning for segmentation should exploit both domain-specific structural similarity across medical volumes and problem-specific local-region distinctiveness, rather than only learning global image-level representations. The authors implement this by introducing novel global contrasting strategies that pair structurally similar slices/volumes and a local contrastive loss that enforces discriminative features for corresponding local regions, then fine-tune the network on limited labeled data; extensive experiments on three MRI datasets show substantial gains over other SSL and semi-supervised methods, achieving near-benchmark performance with only two labeled volumes when combined with simple augmentation.

result.text: The paper addresses noisy and imperfect one-to-one image-text pairing in vision-language pretraining, where strict binary positives/negatives in contrastive CLIP training fails to capture many-to-many or partially matching relationships. Its key insight is that intra-modal fine-grained self-similarities can produce a softened target distribution that lets related but not identical samples share positive mass, thereby providing a soft cross-modal alignment that reflects local similarities while still emphasizing true positives. The method, called SoftCLIP, constructs softened targets from intra-modal self-similarity matrices, disentangles and reweights negative mass to preserve contrastive discrimination, and uses these soft targets to supervise cross-modal alignment during pretraining; this yields large gains (e.g., +6.8%/7.2% ImageNet zero-shot) over CLIP when trained on CC3M/CC12M.
