result.text: The paper addresses unsupervised image/video hashing for compact binary codes without labels, focusing on maximizing each bit's entropy to improve retrieval performance. Its key insight is that entropy is maximized when each bit is balanced (half ones, half zeros), and instead of adding a hard-to-tune entropy term to the loss, one can enforce this balance directly via a parameter-free network layer that steers continuous features toward the ideal half-half bit distribution. The proposed Bi-Half Net layer minimizes a penalized Wasserstein-distance proxy between learned continuous features and the optimal balanced distribution, producing binary codes by pushing feature activations to approximate balanced bit assignments; experiments on multiple image and video benchmarks (FLICKR25K, NUS-WIDE, CIFAR-10, MS COCO, MNIST, UCF-101, HMDB-51) demonstrate compact codes and competitive or superior retrieval performance.

result.text: The paper studies machine unlearning—removing a subset of training data's influence from a trained model—by asking which properties of the forget set make unlearning hard and how algorithms behave on non-random deletion requests. The key insight is that unlearning difficulty is driven by interpretable characteristics of the forget set (e.g., homogeneity, influence, or representativeness) and that evaluating algorithms on forget sets that isolate these factors exposes failure modes invisible with random deletions. args.text: We propose Prototype-Code Memory Cross-Modal Hashing (PCM-CMH), a domain-adaptive framework that couples prototype-anchored alignment on a shared unit hypersphere with a quantization code memory to stabilize training under noisy correspondences and distribution shift. Attribute-conditioned prototypes are learned per class and domain in the continuous space while a momentum-updated memory stores reliable binary codes; a dual-queue contrastive objective aligns instances to cross-modal, cross-domain prototypes and enforces Hamming consistency to their memory codes. A dual self-paced schedule with complementary supervision integrates easy, reliable instances and features first, using momentum-based correspondence correction to avoid reinforcing wrong pairs, while a groupwise Bi-Half regularizer preserves per-attribute bit balance to prevent code collapse. We further refine affinities via intra-modal manifold random walks before committing updates to memory and distill prototypes through quantization-aware mapping to the Hamming hypersphere, yielding robust, balanced codes that transfer across domains.

result.text: The paper examines whether current machine unlearning techniques for large language models (LLMs) truly remove memorized training data or merely suppress its outputs, showing they are vulnerable to "benign relearning" attacks that can jog forgotten memories back into the model. The key insight is that approximate unlearning often leaves latent representations intact so that retraining on a small, loosely related benign dataset can reactivate the suppressed knowledge and recover harmful or verbatim memorized content. The authors formalize an unlearning–relearning pipeline, empirically evaluate it across three unlearning benchmarks (demonstrating recovery of sensitive and copyrighted content using unrelated public data), and analyze attack effectiveness to argue that current methods fail to robustly forget, suggesting the need for stronger, provable unlearning mechanisms and practical guidelines.

We build a heterogeneous cross-modal graph and use alternating intra-modal random walks to refine affinities and discover attribute-consistent neighborhoods; a self-paced curriculum then gradually increases walk depth and the strength of adversarial attribute perturbations, enforcing invariance to allowed edits and sensitivity to flips. Features are aligned on a shared unit hypersphere using comparative, class-agnostic prototypes mined from the refined graph and stabilized by a code-memory quantizer, while a Bi-Half-style balancing layer maintains high-entropy bits during quantization. result.text: The paper addresses the limited scope of existing neural architecture search (NAS) benchmarks, which focus on a few well-studied tasks (e.g., image classification) and thus leave open how NAS methods perform across broadly different domains. Its key insight is that evaluating NAS across a diverse set of tasks reveals robustness issues and can invalidate common conclusions drawn from narrow benchmarks, motivating a standard, diverse evaluation suite. The authors introduce NAS-Bench-360, a curated collection of ten tasks spanning varied domains, dataset sizes, dimensionalities, and objectives that remain compatible with CNN-based search spaces, and for two tasks provide precomputed performance for 15,625 architectures to enable fast, reproducible NAS experiments. Using this suite, they show that modern NAS methods often perform inconsistently and sometimes catastrophically on out-of-distribution tasks, demonstrating the need for more comprehensive benchmarking.

result.text: The paper addresses the high memory cost of KV caching during generative inference with large language models by proposing a plug-and-play way to compress the KV cache without retraining. The key insight is that attention heads exhibit distinct, predictable structures—some focus on local context, some on special tokens, and some attend broadly—so the cache can be adapted per-head to keep only the vectors that matter. The method profiles attention patterns cheaply, then constructs an adaptive KV cache that evicts long-range entries on local-focused heads, drops non-special tokens on special-token-focused heads, and retains full caches for globally attending heads; this profiling-guided FastGen approach reduces GPU memory use substantially while preserving generation quality and requires no expensive fine-tuning.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of machine unlearning for sequences of data deletions that are chosen adaptively in response to published models, a setting where prior non-convex unlearning methods only guarantee correctness for non-adaptive (independent) deletion sequences. The key insight is to reduce adaptive deletion guarantees to non-adaptive ones by leveraging differential privacy and its connection to max-information: a model-training procedure that is differentially private limits how much adaptive deletion choices can depend on published models, so non-adaptive unlearning bounds can be converted into adaptive ones. Concretely, the authors combine this reduction with existing non-adaptive unlearning techniques to produce general algorithms that provide provable deletion guarantees for arbitrary model classes and training methods, and they both theoretically show why earlier non-convex approaches fail under adaptive deletions and empirically demonstrate a practical attack that breaks the SISA algorithm on CIFAR-10, MNIST, and Fashion-MNIST.

result.text: The paper addresses test-time adaptation to distribution shift using only a few unlabeled target samples, aiming to leverage prior knowledge from pretrained foundation models and multiple source domains more effectively than prior methods. The key insight is that a learnable, domain-specific visual prompt distilled from a knowledge bank of source-domain features can steer pretrained features toward a target domain, and that jointly learning this prompting with domain-aware contrastive objectives and meta-learning yields better transfer than disjoint training. Concretely, the method builds a knowledge bank from source-domain features extracted by a frozen backbone, trains a domain prompt generator conditioned on few-shot target examples to compress relevant knowledge into a prompt, and applies the prompt via a guidance module to adapt visual features at test time while optimizing with a domain-aware contrastive loss and meta-learning across domains. result.text: We propose Uncertainty Interaction Shapley (UIS), extending predictive-uncertainty Shapley attributions to higher-order interactions by formulating the entropy-based characteristic function within the weighted least squares (WLS) framework that underlies Shapley interaction indices, yielding a unified objective and estimator. Concretely, we define k-order coefficients that jointly reconstruct conditional-entropy games via optimal WLS and estimate them with a single representation-driven sampler in the spirit of SHAP-IQ, sharing lower-order terms for variance reduction. To compute entropy terms robustly and efficiently, we plug in RKHS conditional-embedding estimators of conditional entropies/mutual informations and derive CLT-style asymptotics and valid confidence intervals by adapting randomized-coalition inference machinery from SPVIM to this WLS setting. The result is a scalable, statistically grounded method to explain which feature interactions drive model uncertainty, enabling targeted acquisition of synergistic features and covariate-shift diagnosis.

result.text: The paper tackles the scalability bottleneck of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training, which is typically restricted to a single GPU and thus cannot handle high-resolution or large-scale scenes; the key insight is that because each Gaussian only contributes to a small, dynamic subset of pixels, training can be distributed by communicating only the required Gaussians to the corresponding pixel partitions and dynamically balancing load. They implement this idea in Grendel, a distributed system that partitions 3DGS parameters across GPUs, uses sparse all-to-all communication to transfer relevant Gaussians to pixel shards, supports batched multi-view training (rather than one view at a time), and applies a simple sqrt(batch size) hyperparameter scaling rule. By enabling dynamic partitioning and sparse communication, Grendel scales 3DGS to tens of millions of Gaussians across many GPUs and demonstrably improves reconstruction quality on large, high-resolution scenes (e.g., raising PSNR from 26.28 to 27.28 on Rubble by moving from 11.2M Gaussians on one GPU to 40.4M on 16 GPUs).

The paper addresses the vulnerability that machine unlearning systems—designed to efficiently remove a user’s data from trained models instead of retraining from scratch—can be forced to incur the full retraining cost, undermining practical guarantees and denial-of-service resistance. Its key insight is that certification formalisms for unlearning often ignore computational budgets, creating an attack surface where carefully crafted training examples (poisoning points) can be made pivotal so that any subsequent removal request for them forces the unlearning mechanism to fall back to expensive retraining. The authors formalize this attack objective, construct poisoning strategies that maximize the likelihood a point becomes influential enough to trigger retraining under common certified unlearning schemes, and empirically validate on standard datasets that small, targeted perturbations in training data substantially increase the rate of full retraining events, thereby demonstrating a realistic and efficient denial-of-service vector against certified machine unlearning.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of test-time adaptation for dense prediction tasks (semantic segmentation and depth estimation), where prior image-level visual prompts obscure spatial details and thus limit domain-specific knowledge extraction. Its key insight is that sparse, pixel-level prompts distributed across the image can preserve spatial context while using only minimal trainable parameters, and that allocating and updating those sparse prompts according to per-pixel distribution shift and per-sample characteristics yields better adaptation. The method, Sparse Visual Domain Prompts (SVDP), places a very small fraction of trainable parameters at selected pixels, with a Domain Prompt Placement (DPP) scheme to allocate parameters to pixels with large domain shift and a Domain Prompt Updating (DPU) strategy that optimizes prompts per target sample during test time. Experiments on standard TTA and continual TTA benchmarks show that SVDP achieves state-of-the-art performance with far fewer tunable parameters.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of over-penalization in evidential neural networks when samples with high data uncertainty are labeled one-hot, which hinders learning reliable uncertainty estimates. The key insight is to use the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) to quantify how informative each sample's evidence is and dynamically reweight training losses so the model focuses on learning representations for uncertain classes rather than being overly punished for noisy labels. Methodologically, they introduce Fisher Information-based Evidential Deep Learning (I-EDL), which computes per-sample Fisher-based weights to adjust evidential Dirichlet-parameter learning and jointly optimizes a PAC-Bayesian bound to improve generalization. result.text: We propose task-conditioned joint architecture-and-weight diffusion that models neural networks as sequences interleaving operation tokens and weight-token latents, conditioned on embeddings from unlabeled target data. result.text: The paper tackles the storage and runtime inefficiency of point-based real-time neural rendering—specifically the large, gigabyte-scale collections of 3D Gaussians produced by SfM that impede scalability and splatting speed. Its key insight is that most Gaussians contribute little to global scene reconstruction and can therefore be identified and compacted without perceptible quality loss by borrowing ideas from network pruning and distillation. The method, LightGaussian, ranks Gaussians by a computed global significance, prunes and recovers low-significance elements, distills higher-degree spherical harmonic coefficients into lower-degree ones using pseudo-view augmentation, and applies significance-aware vector quantization to reduce bitwidth; this pipeline yields about 15× compression and large FPS gains while preserving visual fidelity and generalizes to other Gaussian-based 3D representations.

The key insight is that protecting deleted records requires ensuring the privacy of the remaining records as well—privacy of existing data is necessary for privacy of deletions—and that sound deletion guarantees must account for adaptive deletion behavior and cumulative leakage. The key insight is that by defining a simple, analytically tractable premetric one can construct closed-form target vector fields for flow matching that generalize the Euclidean case to arbitrary geometries, removing the need for divergence computation and simulation on many domains. args.text: We propose Wasserstein Prompt Fields (WPF) for dense continual test-time adaptation in vision–language models, modeling domain shift as a spatially varying, low-parameter prompt field attached to pixels that transports per-pixel features from a source-domain barycenter to the evolving target. Concretely, we build a per-pixel feature bank over multiple source domains and compute a Wasserstein barycenter as a style prior; at test time, we estimate a low-rank optimal transport map from this barycenter to the target using unlabeled images and update only the sparse prompt field under a trust-region constraint. To stabilize adaptation without labels, we employ swapped-prediction consistency between an online and EMA prompt head and a homeostatic gate that blends shared low-rank with plastic high-rank prompt components per region to mitigate forgetting. WPF enables fast, label-free adaptation for segmentation and depth while accommodating target label-proportion shifts via the OT objective.

result.text: We propose TriMed-Struct: a unified pretraining framework that jointly learns from 2D slices, 3D volumes, and accompanying radiology reports by coupling local masked modeling with global graph-structured constraints across patients and modalities. Specifically, we introduce cross-modality masked volume modeling that conditions on observed modalities and an explicit modality mask to reconstruct masked-out modality tokens at both slice and volume levels, while enforcing slice–volume clustering agreement and masked-embedding prediction for robust 2D–3D consistency. A graph-matching structural loss aligns patient-level embeddings aggregated over modalities and text (via masked report completion) to preserve global pathology relationships, and an auxiliary intermediate-layer alignment objective ties the 2D and 3D branches to learn reusable mid-level features. We hypothesize this tri-modal structural SSL substantially improves label efficiency for segmentation and cross-modality synthesis, outperforming image-only or text-only pretraining across diverse medical benchmarks.

result.text: Manifold-to-Prototype Self-Paced Cross-Modal Hashing (MaP-SCMH) is a three-stage curriculum for robust cross-modal hashing under noisy correspondences and domain shift. Stage 1 mines intra-modal affinities via bi-directional random walks on modality-specific graphs to obtain graph-consistent pseudo-similarities and trains hash codes with a parameter-free bit-balance layer and a code-memory contrastive objective for stable, high-entropy quantization. Stage 2 aligns the modalities by learning prototype-anchored features on a shared unit hypersphere and supervising quantization so that relations are preserved when mapping to a Hamming hypersphere. Stage 3 activates a complementary-supervision head with momentum-based correspondence correction, whose accepted pairs are scheduled by instance- and feature-level self-paced weights so the model gradually absorbs harder, corrected pairs while filtering noise.

result.text: The paper examines whether model providers can dishonestly claim to have performed machine unlearning while still retaining information about the removed data, showing that existing verification techniques are fragile. Its key insight is that current verification strategies fall into two broad types and both can be evaded by carefully designed adversarial unlearning processes that preserve utility yet hide remnants of the target data from verifiers. The authors propose two novel adversarial unlearning methods that intentionally manipulate model updates to pass verification checks while keeping predictive influence of the removed data, and they support these attacks with theoretical analysis and experiments on real-world datasets demonstrating practical success. Their results reveal fundamental vulnerabilities in present unlearning verification approaches and motivate stronger, more robust verification and defense mechanisms.

result.text: The paper addresses efficient long-video understanding with vision-language LLMs by tackling the computational bottleneck from vast numbers of video tokens. Its key insight is to encode videos streamingly into a small set of propagated, question-relevant memories rather than repeatedly processing all frames, preserving temporal context without excessive token cost. Methodologically, VideoStreaming segments videos into clips and uses Memory-Propagated Streaming Encoding to merge each clip with a distilled historical memory, then applies Adaptive Memory Selection to pick a constant number of question-related memories to feed the LLM for reasoning. This disentangled extraction-and-reasoning design reduces redundancy, enables precise temporal question answering, and yields improved accuracy and efficiency on long-video benchmarks.

args.text: Certified Prototype-Smoothed Cross-Modal Hashing (Cert-PSCMH) provides retrieval guarantees under both input perturbations and bit flips by jointly smoothing in feature and Hamming spaces. We learn prototype-anchored, unit-sphere features that are quantized with a bit-balance layer and a code-memory contrastive objective; at test time, we apply Bernoulli bit-flip smoothing to codes and Gaussian smoothing to features, deriving certified Hamming radii and l_infinity radii via an infinity-to-2 operator-norm bound of the feature map. Training maximizes certified margins to incorrect prototypes under the smoothed distributions and is scheduled with self-paced instance/feature weights to remain robust to noisy correspondences. This yields certifiable top-k retrieval stability across modalities while retaining competitive retrieval accuracy.

The key insight is that failures arise from the sampler rather than the learned model, and that viewing diffusion models as energy-based (score) models enables richer composition and sampling strategies. The authors introduce an energy-based parameterization of diffusion models plus MCMC-inspired samplers—including Metropolis-corrected updates and new compositional operators—that reuse pretrained components to perform more accurate, stable compositional generation, demonstrating improvements on tasks like classifier-guided ImageNet and compositional text-to-image synthesis.

The provider proves in a recursive SNARK that the released weights equal retraining on the originally committed dataset with the requested records removed, and simultaneously that evaluation on a regulator-committed secret audit distribution (including trigger-augmented inputs) stays within bounded deviation and does not realize any targeted misclassification on committed trigger sets—revealing neither data, weights, nor audit contents. The protocol composes with DP-SGD and adaptive-deletion reductions so proofs remain sound and privacy-preserving under sequences of adaptively chosen deletions, and recursive aggregation keeps costs practical over many requests. This closes the verification gap and mitigates unlearning-enabled backdoor insertion while addressing known fragility of current unlearning verifiers.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of learning flexible probability distributions on data that lie on Riemannian manifolds (e.g., spheres, tori, hyperbolic spaces), where standard normalizing flows—built for Euclidean (flat) spaces—are misspecified and perform poorly. Its key insight is that continuous normalizing flows can be generalized to Riemannian manifolds by defining the flow as the solution of an ODE whose vector field respects the manifold geometry, allowing exact transformation of densities via the manifold-aware continuity equation rather than flat-space change-of-variable formulas. The method parameterizes a time-dependent tangent-vector field on the manifold, integrates the induced ODE to push a base density along manifold-respecting trajectories, and computes log-density changes using the Riemannian divergence (trace of the covariant derivative) to train the model; experiments show substantial improvements over Euclidean and projected-flow baselines on synthetic and real datasets.

result.text: The paper addresses unsupervised domain adaptation under Generalized Target Shift (GeTarS), where both class-conditional distributions and label proportions differ between source and target domains, a setting poorly handled by existing methods that force representation invariance. The key insight is to avoid insisting on invariant features and instead learn an explicit optimal transport map in a pretrained representation space that directly maps source representations to target ones, which can simultaneously align conditional distributions and recover target label proportions. Methodologically, they parameterize the optimal transport map as a neural network trained to push source representations to match the target distribution while preserving class-conditional structure, and provide theoretical guarantees of uniqueness, conditional matching, proportion recovery, and controlled target risk under mild assumptions. Empirically, this flexible, scalable approach outperforms prior GeTarS methods across multiple datasets.

args.text: We propose BPA-CLIP: a batchwise Procrustes-aligned contrastive objective that explicitly removes modality-specific rotations and scalings that contribute to the modality gap. At each training step, we center and whiten image/text embeddings, estimate the optimal orthogonal map aligning one modality to the other (orthogonal Procrustes), and penalize the post-alignment residual while lightly regularizing the map toward identity to avoid overfitting. This aligns higher-order neighborhood structure beyond pairwise scores and pairs naturally with the standard contrastive loss; a geodesic hard-negative schedule maintains uniformity as alignment tightens. Compared to similarity-consistency regularization, BPA-CLIP targets the batchwise subspace mismatch implicated by gap analyses and is expected to improve cross-modal interchangeability, zero-shot retrieval/classification, and fairness sensitivity.

result.text: The paper tackles unsupervised domain adaptive hashing for image retrieval, where transferring semantic structure from a labelled source to an unlabelled target while producing compact hash codes is challenging because prior adaptations either naively reuse domain-adaptation tactics or align features in Hamming space with limited semantic fidelity. The key insight is to learn a domain-shared unit hypersphere of prototype-anchored, contrastively trained features that are both uniformly distributed and resistant to category conflicts, then map those continuous features to a Hamming hypersphere so that semantic relations are preserved during quantization. Methodologically, Comparative Prototype Hashing (CPH) constructs class prototypes and performs prototype contrastive learning across domains to eliminate domain gaps in the shared hypersphere, supervises hashing with dual-domain similarity information, and finally maps features to binary codes on a Hamming hypersphere; this yields substantially improved cross-domain and single-domain retrieval performance on benchmarks like Office-Home and Office-31.

result.text: This paper addresses the security risk that machine unlearning—designed to remove specific data from trained models—can be abused to implant backdoors, so that the unlearned model misbehaves in the presence of a trigger. The key insight is that selectively removing particular contributed examples (or combining minor upfront poisoning with later unlearning) can shift model decision boundaries in a controlled way, enabling backdoor activation without obvious tampering of the original training set. The authors propose two attack methods: a pure-unlearning attack that achieves a backdoor solely by submitting malicious unlearning requests for a small subset of the attacker’s contributed data, and a hybrid attack that first plants a few poisoned examples with a trigger and then activates the backdoor via unlearning; both optimize attack utility while maintaining stealth. They empirically validate these attacks across multiple unlearning algorithms, model architectures, and datasets, showing that unlearning mechanisms can be exploited to reliably and covertly insert backdoors.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of building flexible, general-purpose normalizing flows that respect non‑Euclidean data geometry without requiring handcrafted, manifold‑specific layers. Its key insight is that Neural ODEs can be generalized to arbitrary manifolds using only local geometric information, enabling continuous-time flows whose dynamics remain on the manifold and whose probability densities can be tracked via a continuous change-of-variables formula. The authors introduce Neural Manifold ODEs and use them to construct Manifold Continuous Normalizing Flows (MCNFs), which integrate vector fields defined in local charts (or via embeddings) to transport probability mass while computing log-densities through an ODE for the instantaneous change of variables. Empirically, MCNFs are simple to apply across different manifolds and produce improved density estimation and downstream task performance compared with prior manifold-specific flow designs.

result.text: The paper addresses Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA), where a source model must adapt to continuously changing unlabeled target domains without access to source data, a setting in which self-training with noisy pseudo-labels leads to error accumulation and catastrophic forgetting. The key insight is to shift adaptation from altering model parameters to learning lightweight image-layer visual prompts that reformulate inputs for the frozen source model, thereby preserving source knowledge while capturing domain-specific shifts. The method designs two complementary prompt types—domain-specific prompts to encode current-domain characteristics and domain-agnostic prompts to retain shared knowledge—and introduces a homeostasis-based adaptation strategy that suppresses domain-sensitive parameters in the agnostic prompts to better learn invariant features. This model-free prompt learning approach avoids forgetting and error accumulation and yields substantial gains over prior CTTA methods on CIFAR-10C, CIFAR-100C, ImageNet-C, and VLCS benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses how to represent 3D rotations in deep learning models, questioning why symmetric orthogonalization via SVD—commonly used in traditional vision for projecting matrices onto O(n)/SO(n)—is rarely used as a learned rotation representation despite the lack of a universally best alternative. The authors provide a theoretical analysis justifying SVD for projection onto SO(3) and empirically validate the approach by replacing standard representations with SVD orthogonalization across a range of supervised and unsupervised vision tasks, showing it achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of efficiently producing task-specific neural architectures for previously unseen tasks, avoiding costly per-task search or poor transfers from architectures found on other tasks. Its key insight is that a task-aware architecture controller combined with meta-learned shared weights can both propose suitable architectures and quickly adapt their parameters to new tasks, because meta-weights capture a good initialization across diverse tasks and architectures. Experimental results on toy regression and few-shot classification show M-NAS outperforms baselines in producing effective task-aware architectures with much greater efficiency.

result.text: ZK-SafeUnlearn: augment publicly verifiable unlearning with a zero-knowledge safety audit that certifies both correct deletion and absence of attacker-chosen backdoor behaviors after unlearning. The provider proves in a recursive SNARK that the released weights equal retraining on the originally committed dataset with the requested records removed, and simultaneously that evaluation on a regulator-committed secret audit distribution (including trigger-augmented inputs) stays within bounded deviation and does not realize any targeted misclassification on committed trigger sets—revealing neither data, weights, nor audit contents. The protocol composes with DP-SGD and adaptive-deletion reductions so proofs remain sound and privacy-preserving under sequences of adaptively chosen deletions, and recursive aggregation keeps costs practical over many requests. This closes the verification gap and mitigates unlearning-enabled backdoor insertion while addressing known fragility of current unlearning verifiers.

args.text: We propose Conformal Premetric Flow Matching (CPFM), which jointly learns a scalar conformal factor over the ambient space and a time-dependent vector field by flow matching on the induced Riemannian manifold, marrying CM-CNFs’ tractable conformal volume accounting with the simulation-free training of Riemannian flow matching and probability-path divergence. Target velocity fields are defined under the learned conformal metric via closed-form constructions (e.g., score/Stein fields of geodesic Gaussian or heat-kernel interpolation paths), while curvature is regularized with a Laplacian penalty and the metric is anchored to Euclidean outside data regions to improve OOD behavior. Training aligns the vector field to these targets without integrating trajectories; at test time, exact likelihoods are obtained by integrating the conformal log-density ODE once, while fast sampling uses explicit integrators with step sizes adapted to learned local curvature. On thin-manifold datasets, CPFM aims to reduce function evaluations and improve likelihoods versus CM-CNFs and RFM, with ablations showing the learned geometry concentrates mass near the data while preserving angle structure.

result.text: The paper addresses test-time adaptation for vision-language models, aiming to improve zero-shot generalization to unlabeled target-domain images without costly backbone fine-tuning. The key insight is that leveraging self-supervised contrastive learning between prompt-conditioned representations—rather than only entropy minimization—can better exploit pre-trained model features and retain historical knowledge to stabilize adaptation. SwapPrompt implements this via dual prompts (an online prompt and a temporally averaged target prompt) and a swapped prediction mechanism where the online prompt with one augmented view predicts the class assignments produced by the target prompt with an alternative view, using contrastive objectives to refine the online prompt; this lightweight, model-agnostic approach yields state-of-the-art TTA results on ImageNet and multiple datasets and approaches supervised prompt adaptation performance.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of extending Shapley-value explanations to reliably quantify higher-order feature interactions (Shapley Interaction Index, SII) by showing whether and how SII can be derived as the optimum of a weighted least squares (WLS) approximation, closing a long-standing theoretical gap that previously motivated alternative interaction indices. The key insight is that SII together with lower-order k-Shapley values form the coefficients of an optimal WLS reconstruction of a game, analogous to how the Shapley value minimizes a specific WLS for single-feature attributions; the authors prove this equivalence for the Shapley value and pairwise interactions and present empirically supported conjectures for higher orders. Methodologically, they derive the appropriate weighting scheme and closed-form characterization, then implement KernelSHAP-IQ—a direct extension of KernelSHAP that solves the resulting WLS to estimate interaction attributions—and validate it empirically to achieve state-of-the-art performance for detecting and quantifying feature interactions.

args.text: Event-Guided Object Memory for Streaming Video-LLMs (E-GOM) uses sparse event streams (or frame-to-event surrogates) to maintain a low-cost temporal saliency signal that drives object-centric updates and attention routing. Hyper Histogram-style event features trigger change-point detection and feed a slot-based tracker/dynamics prior so that only active entities refresh while inactive ones persist, replacing dense frame tokens with compact predictive slots. On the language side, we keep a small recent window plus entity-indexed sink KVs and invoke high-res frame encoders with mixture-of-depths only when event statistics or question-conditioned uncertainty exceed a threshold; otherwise the model reasons over event-updated slots alone. Trained with segment-level temporal supervision, E-GOM delivers constant memory, sub-frame temporal precision, and improved moment localization/QA on long videos.

result.text: The paper addresses learning cross-modal tasks when paired multi-modal data is scarce by studying why pre-trained multi-modal contrastive spaces still exhibit a modality gap that prevents embeddings from different modalities being truly interchangeable. The key insight is a theoretical characterization of the contrastive embedding geometry that reveals persistent modality-specific structure, and that explicitly connecting modalities, collapsing intra-modality variance, and introducing controlled corruption can align those spaces to improve interchangeability. The authors propose C^3 (Connect, Collapse, Corrupt): connect by synthesizing or mapping anchors across modalities to create alignment pairs, collapse by reducing within-modality dispersion so representations occupy a shared subspace, and corrupt by applying noise/augmentation to encourage robustness and overlap between modalities. Evaluated on zero-shot image/audio/video captioning and text-to-image generation, C^3 substantially closes the modality gap and yields state-of-the-art cross-modal performance using only uni-modal data.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of compressing large numbers of Gaussians and their attributes in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for novel view synthesis, where existing methods compress each Gaussian independently and ignore spatial interactions. The key insight is to apply an anchor-level autoregressive context model—grouping anchors into multiple levels so that uncoded anchors can be predicted from already coded anchors in coarser levels—to exploit inter-anchor dependencies and improve entropy modeling. Methodologically, they implement this multilevel context prediction and additionally introduce a low-dimensional quantized feature as a hyperprior per anchor to efficiently code levels with few or no prior anchors, enabling more effective entropy coding. The approach achieves over 100× size reduction versus vanilla 3DGS and ~15× versus recent Scaffold-GS while maintaining comparable or better rendering quality.

result.text: The paper addresses unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) for large pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs), focusing on how to reduce source–target distribution shift while avoiding brittle prompt engineering. result.text: We propose Partial-OT CLIP: augment contrastive image–text pretraining with a mini-batch partial optimal transport regularizer that softly aligns only the most reliable cross-modal pairs beyond the labeled matches, encouraging overlap of image and text embedding subspaces while avoiding spurious correspondences. result.text: The paper addresses the practical challenge of choosing and using 3D rotation representations in machine learning, where many equivalent mathematical forms exist but they differ markedly in behavior for gradient-based optimization. Its key insight is that different representations (e.g., Euler angles, axis-angle, quaternions, rotation matrices, and learned parameterizations) have distinct geometric and numerical properties—such as continuity, singularities, redundancy, and constraints—that systematically affect learning depending on whether rotations are inputs or outputs and whether angles are small. The authors survey these properties, consolidate empirical and theoretical findings about which issues (discontinuities, antipodal symmetry, parameter overconstraint, projection needs) matter in practice, and provide concrete guidance and recommendations: use minimal unconstrained representations or continuous 4D embeddings for outputs to avoid singularities, prefer stable embeddings for inputs, and exploit small-angle approximations when applicable, along with practical methods like normalization, regularization, and loss design to handle constraints.

result.text: The paper addresses the long-standing gap between lower and upper bounds for oracle complexity of high-order algorithms in smooth convex minimization, where previous methods achieved the optimal rate up to an extra log factor due to costly binary-search subroutines. The key insight is that the extra logarithmic factor is not intrinsic but an artifact of existing algorithmic designs, and it can be removed by constructing an algorithm that avoids binary search while preserving the accelerated convergence mechanism. The authors propose a novel high-order acceleration scheme that carefully integrates higher-order model-based steps with a non-iterative step-size/accuracy control, yielding the first method whose p-th order oracle complexity matches the lower bound Theta(epsilon^{-2/(3p+1)}). This result both closes the theoretical optimality gap and provides a more practical blueprint for accelerated high-order optimization.

result.text: We propose Conformal Metric Continuous Normalizing Flows (CM-CNFs), which learn a scalar conformal factor over the ambient space to define a Riemannian metric that warps volumes around the data, and evolve a continuous-time flow whose dynamics and log-density updates are computed with respect to this learned geometry. Because conformal metrics admit closed-form adjustments to divergence and volume elements relative to Euclidean space, we can track exact likelihoods w.r.t. Lebesgue measure while jointly learning geometry (the conformal factor) and transport (the vector field) in continuous time. This unifies conformal-embedding approaches that preserve angles with manifold CNFs that assume a known manifold, enabling the model to approximate distributions supported near unknown thin manifolds without sacrificing tractable change-of-variables. We evaluate CM-CNFs on synthetic and real manifold-structured data, ablating geometry-only, transport-only, and joint training to show improved density estimation, OOD detection, and robustness to curvature.

result.text: The paper studies the “modality gap,” a geometric phenomenon where different data modalities (e.g., images and text) occupy distinct, arm’s-length regions in the shared embedding space of multi-modal contrastive models like CLIP, which can hinder downstream performance and fairness. The key insight is that this gap arises from two interacting causes: (1) standard neural network initialization biases each encoder’s outputs into a narrow cone so that different encoders start separated, and (2) contrastive optimization—particularly the temperature hyperparameter—preserves or enforces a nonzero separation between modalities during training. To analyze and mitigate this, the authors combine empirical measurement and theoretical analysis of initialization-induced concentration with controlled contrastive training experiments that vary temperature and alignment forces, showing that adjusting the modality gap can substantially affect zero-shot classification accuracy and fairness outcomes.

The key insight is to combine a parametric human body model with temporal and multi-view attention mechanisms so that tracked skeletal motion guides robust aggregation of visual evidence across time and views, enabling generalization to unseen identities and poses. Concretely, Neural Human Performer first uses a temporal transformer to fuse tracked, body-aligned features over time according to skeletal motion, then applies a multi-view transformer that cross-attends between these temporally-fused features and pixel-aligned features from each camera at each timestep to integrate multi-view observations on the fly and predict radiance fields. Experiments on ZJU-MoCap and AIST demonstrate substantial improvements over recent generalizable NeRF approaches for novel humans and poses.

result.text: The paper examines whether current machine unlearning techniques for large language models (LLMs) truly remove memorized training data or merely suppress its outputs, showing they are vulnerable to "benign relearning" attacks that can jog forgotten memories back into the model. The key insight is that approximate unlearning often leaves latent representations intact so that retraining on a small, loosely related benign dataset can reactivate the suppressed knowledge and recover harmful or verbatim memorized content. The authors formalize an unlearning–relearning pipeline, empirically evaluate it across three unlearning benchmarks (demonstrating recovery of sensitive and copyrighted content using unrelated public data), and analyze attack effectiveness to argue that current methods fail to robustly forget, suggesting the need for stronger, provable unlearning mechanisms and practical guidelines.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of learning generative models on complex manifolds (e.g., spheres, tori, implicit surfaces) where existing Euclidean flow methods are either geometry-restricted or computationally costly. The key insight is to parameterize the model density directly as a source (prior) density minus the divergence of a neural network, because divergence is a local linear differential operator that is straightforward to compute on manifolds and sidesteps costly ODE-based change-of-variable computations. The resulting Moser Flow is a continuous normalizing flow whose training does not require backpropagation through an ODE solver, yields an explicit density representation that improves fidelity, and is provably a universal density approximator under mild assumptions. Empirically, Moser Flow enables the first effective flow-based sampling on general curved surfaces and outperforms existing CNFs in density estimation, sample quality, and training efficiency on synthetic and real-world geoscience benchmarks.

We propose Conformal Premetric Flow Matching (CPFM), which learns a scalar conformal factor over the ambient space to induce an analytically tractable premetric that flattens thin data manifolds, while training a velocity field via Riemannian flow matching in this learned geometry. Lebesgue measure despite the changing metric, and we alternate updates between geometry (conformal factor) and transport (velocity) to decouple support learning from density learning. The method, CLIPood, introduces Margin Metric Softmax (MMS), which assigns class-adaptive margins in a metric-softmax loss to respect inter-class semantic relations during fine-tuning, and Beta Moving Average (BMA), a temporal ensemble that weights and combines the pre-trained zero-shot and fine-tuned models according to a Beta-distributed schedule. Empirically, this combination consistently outperforms existing generalization techniques across diverse datasets and OOD scenarios.

result.text: The paper addresses robust 6D object pose estimation by framing point cloud registration as a probabilistic denoising diffusion process on the SE(3) manifold to handle real-world noise and occlusion. The key insight is to perform diffusion and reverse (denoising) processes directly in SE(3) using its Lie algebra se(3), which allows meaningful, constrained perturbations and refinements of rigid transformations rather than treating poses as vectors in Euclidean space. Methodologically, they define an SE(3) forward process that gradually perturbs the optimal rigid transform via perturbation transformations in se(3), derive a registration-specific variational lower bound to train an SE(3) denoising network that iteratively recovers the clean transform, and show the denoiser can be implemented as a surrogate registration model compatible with different deep registration backbones, achieving strong results on TUD-L, LINEMOD, and Occluded-LINEMOD.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of explaining model uncertainty for differentiable probabilistic models, extending beyond a single counterfactual explanation (CLUE) to capture the range and diversity of plausible uncertainty-reducing edits. The key insight is that many individual CLUEs within a local latent neighborhood are redundant, so meaningful explanations require both diverse representative counterfactuals and amortised mappings that generalise across groups of uncertain inputs. Methodologically, the authors define δ-CLUE to characterise the set of latent counterfactuals within a δ-ball, introduce ∇-CLUE to select a diverse subset of distinct uncertainty-reducing explanations, and propose GLAM-CLUE to learn amortised functions that transform whole groups of uncertain inputs into certain ones in one forward pass; experiments demonstrate these approaches reduce redundancy and improve the usefulness and efficiency of uncertainty explanations.

args.text: We propose Head-Entity Adaptive Caching (HEAC) for streaming Video-LLMs: an entity-indexed KV cache that allocates memory per attention head and per tracked object based on predicted future utility. A lightweight head profiler labels heads as local/global/special and, together with a slot-dynamics prior over objects, drives a budgeted router that retains full KVs only for high-utility head–entity pairs, compresses low-utility pairs into low-rank sketches, and drops the rest while always preserving sink/question heads. The entity states update streamingly and emit change-point events to the LLM, and training uses segment-level supervision with counterfactual rollouts to penalize evictions that harm downstream answers. By aligning KV retention to both transformer head roles and object relevance over time, HEAC attains constant memory with minimal accuracy loss on long-horizon video QA and grounding.

result.text: The paper addresses unreliable predictions in cross-modal retrieval caused by aleatoric uncertainty from low-quality or ambiguous data (e.g., corrupted images, fast videos, vague text). Its key insight is to model this data-induced uncertainty explicitly by representing modality semantics with multiple learnable prototypes and mapping evidence on those prototypes to a principled evidential framework (using Dempster–Shafer and Subjective Logic) that yields Dirichlet-distributed beliefs rather than point estimates. The method builds prototype banks for each modality, aggregates evidence per sample to parameterize Dirichlet distributions over similarity-based beliefs, and fuses those beliefs via the evidential theory to quantify uncertainty and produce more reliable retrieval scores. Experiments on MSR-VTT, MSVD, DiDeMo, and MS-COCO show that this Prototype-based Aleatoric Uncertainty (PAU) approach improves uncertainty estimation and retrieval reliability.

result.text: The paper addresses the limited scope of existing neural architecture search (NAS) benchmarks, which focus on a few well-studied tasks (e.g., image classification) and thus leave open how NAS methods perform across broadly different domains. Its key insight is that evaluating NAS across a diverse set of tasks reveals robustness issues and can invalidate common conclusions drawn from narrow benchmarks, motivating a standard, diverse evaluation suite. The authors introduce NAS-Bench-360, a curated collection of ten tasks spanning varied domains, dataset sizes, dimensionalities, and objectives that remain compatible with CNN-based search spaces, and for two tasks provide precomputed performance for 15,625 architectures to enable fast, reproducible NAS experiments. Using this suite, they show that modern NAS methods often perform inconsistently and sometimes catastrophically on out-of-distribution tasks, demonstrating the need for more comprehensive benchmarking.

args.text: We propose Conformal Probability-Path Flow Matching (CPPF): jointly learn a scalar conformal factor that induces a Riemannian metric around the data and a time-dependent vector field, but train the field without ODE solves by minimizing a probability path divergence written with the conformal divergence and volume form. Choosing target density paths that are geodesically straight under the learned metric yields closed-form target vector fields akin to Riemannian flow matching, while the conformal structure preserves exact likelihoods w.r.t. Lebesgue via known volume scaling. This couples unknown-manifold adaptation (through the conformal metric) with simulation-free PDE matching (through probability-path training), enabling models that concentrate along thin manifolds yet remain tractable. We provide efficient estimators of conformal divergence via spectral bases or Hutchinson tricks and regularize curvature to avoid degenerate warpings.

args.text: We propose Uncertainty-Adaptive Partial-OT CLIP, which couples in-batch partial optimal transport soft matching with per-sample contrastive temperatures driven by evidential aleatoric uncertainty. Concretely, lightweight prototype-based evidential heads on the image and text encoders estimate sample uncertainty and local density; these signals jointly set each example’s partial-transport mass budget and InfoNCE temperature via learned monotone schedules optimized under a robust objective, so ambiguous or low-density samples transport less mass and are contrasted more softly while confident, reliable samples receive sharper alignment. We further stabilize training with cross-/in-modal geometric consistency regularization and uncertainty-aware hard-negative shaping. This design targets web-scale noise and the modality gap, yielding more interchangeable embeddings, stronger long-tail transfer, and calibrated retrieval confidence.

result.text: The paper addresses limitations of randomized smoothing for certifiable robustness beyond the standard isotropic Gaussian case, focusing on how the certified ℓ_p radius scales with input dimension d. The key insight is that for a broad class of i.i.d. smoothing distributions the maximum certifiable ℓ_p radius necessarily shrinks with dimension — for p>2 it decays as O(1/d^{1/2-1/p}) and for many natural non-Gaussian smoothers the decay is even worse — so Gaussian smoothing is essentially optimal (up to constants) for p≥2. The authors prove lower bounds on the achievable certified radius for i.i.d. and generalized Gaussian smoothers and complementary upper bounds for other distributions (e.g., uniform in ℓ_1 or ℓ_∞ balls), and validate these theoretical scaling laws with CIFAR experiments, demonstrating a fundamental “curse of dimensionality” for smoothing-based certification in high dimensions.

args.text: We propose First-Hitting Flow Matching (FHFM), a manifold-aware continuous flow that terminates at an instance-dependent random time defined as the first hitting of a learned absorbing set that approximates the data support. We construct target conditioned bridges via a Doob h-transform built from heat-kernel/spectral approximations of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on the manifold, and train the vector field by flow matching to these bridges while marginalizing over hitting times; in Euclidean or unknown-geometry settings we pair this with a lightweight learned premetric to keep training simulation-free. At inference, trajectories integrate only until first hit, enforcing constraints and accelerating sampling on curved or bounded domains. This unifies first-hitting diffusion’s instance-dependent stopping with Riemannian flow matching and probability-path training, yielding fewer steps and stronger likelihoods on manifold benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses category-level 3D object pose estimation from partial point clouds, tackling the common multihypothesis problem where incomplete observations yield multiple plausible poses. The key insight is to reframe pose estimation as conditional generative modeling rather than direct point-wise regression, using score-based diffusion to capture the full multimodal posterior over poses and thus represent uncertainty and symmetries naturally. Methodologically, GenPose samples many pose candidates from a conditional diffusion model, filters out outliers via likelihood estimation, and mean-pools the remaining samples to produce a final estimate; to make likelihood evaluation practical, the authors train an energy-based model derived from the score model for end-to-end likelihood scoring. The approach attains state-of-the-art results on REAL275, shows strong generalization to novel symmetric categories without fine-tuning, and adapts to pose-tracking tasks with competitive performance.

result.text: The paper tackles uncertainty quantification for deterministic neural networks, aiming to provide fast, scalable estimates that separate aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty without requiring Bayesian or ensemble methods. The key insight is to use a Nadaraya–Watson nonparametric estimator of the conditional label distribution in the model’s feature (embedding) space, which yields principled uncertainty measures and an explicit decomposition between data (aleatoric) and model/coverage (epistemic) uncertainty. The method computes kernel-weighted label distributions around a test point in embedding space and derives uncertainty metrics from that distribution, operating directly on features produced by any pretrained network. Experiments on text classification and image benchmarks (MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-100, ImageNet variants) show the approach is effective and scalable for uncertainty estimation.

args.text: We propose Evidential-Temperature CLIP (ET-CLIP): estimate per-pair aleatoric uncertainty in image–text matching via prototype-based evidential similarities and use it to modulate both pairwise temperature and label softness within a unified contrastive loss. Concretely, modality-specific prototype banks produce Dirichlet beliefs over matches whose concentration scales the InfoNCE temperature and loss weight, while the Dirichlet mean induces soft positive mass over semantically close samples derived from intra-modal neighborhoods. A curriculum anneals a global temperature to reduce modality-cone separation while keeping high-uncertainty pairs hot, and applies a symmetric cross-modal consistency penalty only to low-uncertainty mismatches. This uncertainty-adaptive tempering targets the temperature-driven modality gap and improves zero-shot and retrieval reliability on noisy web data.

result.text: The paper addresses learning image classifiers with provable robustness to Gaussian input perturbations by improving the pretraining stage for models used in randomized smoothing. The key insight is that jointly denoising additive Gaussian noise and reconstructing randomly masked patches forces a Transformer encoder to learn semantics that are inherently robust to Gaussian corruption and thus well-suited as the backbone for Gaussian-smoothed certified classifiers. Methodologically, they introduce Denoising Masked AutoEncoders (DMAE): add Gaussian noise to pixel values, randomly mask patches, and train a Transformer encoder–decoder to reconstruct the original image; the pretrained encoder is then used in smoothed classifiers for which certified radii can be computed analytically. Empirically, DMAE yields substantial gains in certified accuracy—matching or exceeding prior work with a much smaller ViT-Base and setting a new state-of-the-art with ViT-Large on ImageNet, while also transferring well to CIFAR-10.

result.text: The paper tackles few-shot language coordination: enabling a lead agent to rapidly adapt its language to communicate effectively with a population of interlocutors who have varied and previously unseen linguistic abilities. The key insight is that explicitly modeling partners’ mental states—i.e., giving the speaker a theory-of-mind (ToM) that predicts a listener’s beliefs and likely reactions—lets the speaker anticipate how utterances will be interpreted and thus craft more concise, goal-directed instructions. Methodologically, the authors train speakers that incorporate a learned ToM module to simulate listeners’ responses and use those simulations to guide generation, and they evaluate this approach in both a referential game and a language navigation task, showing improved coordination with novel agents compared to non-ToM baselines.

The paper addresses how hierarchical credit assignment in biologically plausible neural networks can be achieved when top-down feedback signals are strong and noisy, contrasting with prior methods that require vanishingly small feedback. The key insight is that learning can be reframed as minimizing the amount of corrective feedback a controller must supply to drive network outputs to targets, so weight updates aim to reduce reliance on external control rather than directly chasing output loss. Methodologically, the authors extend Deep Feedback Control (DFC) to operate with strong feedback, derive local-in-space-and-time learning rules that allow simultaneous learning of forward and feedback connections, and validate the approach on vision benchmarks showing competitive performance and robustness to noise. This yields a novel optimization perspective—learning as control minimization—that avoids biologically unrealistic assumptions about infinitesimal feedback.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of standard diffusion generative models that run to a fixed deterministic time and are ill-suited for data that lie on manifolds, graphs, or categorical spaces. Its key insight is to replace fixed-time termination with a random first-hitting time, enabling instance-dependent stop times that naturally respect constraints of continuous manifolds and discrete/structured domains while accelerating sampling. Methodologically, the authors train First Hitting Diffusion Models (FHDM) by maximum likelihood on diffusion trajectories conditioned to hit observed data via conditional first-hitting bridges derived from Doob’s h-transform (instead of time reversal), and demonstrate this framework across point clouds, spherical climate/geography data, unweighted graphs, and high-dimensional segmentation maps. Empirically, FHDM yields higher-quality samples with fewer diffusion steps compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

result.text: We propose Uncertainty Interaction Shapley (UIS), extending predictive-uncertainty Shapley attributions to higher-order interactions by formulating the entropy-based characteristic function within the weighted least squares (WLS) framework that underlies Shapley interaction indices, yielding a unified objective and estimator. Concretely, we define k-order coefficients that jointly reconstruct conditional-entropy games via optimal WLS and estimate them with a single representation-driven sampler in the spirit of SHAP-IQ, sharing lower-order terms for variance reduction. To compute entropy terms robustly and efficiently, we plug in RKHS conditional-embedding estimators of conditional entropies/mutual informations and derive CLT-style asymptotics and valid confidence intervals by adapting randomized-coalition inference machinery from SPVIM to this WLS setting. The result is a scalable, statistically grounded method to explain which feature interactions drive model uncertainty, enabling targeted acquisition of synergistic features and covariate-shift diagnosis.

result.text: The paper tackles few-shot language coordination: enabling a lead agent to rapidly adapt its language to communicate effectively with a population of interlocutors who have varied and previously unseen linguistic abilities. The key insight is that explicitly modeling partners’ mental states—i.e., giving the speaker a theory-of-mind (ToM) that predicts a listener’s beliefs and likely reactions—lets the speaker anticipate how utterances will be interpreted and thus craft more concise, goal-directed instructions. Methodologically, the authors train speakers that incorporate a learned ToM module to simulate listeners’ responses and use those simulations to guide generation, and they evaluate this approach in both a referential game and a language navigation task, showing improved coordination with novel agents compared to non-ToM baselines.

The paper addresses how to give target propagation (TP)—a biologically plausible alternative to backpropagation—solid mathematical foundations and fix its practical limitations, especially in non-invertible networks where difference target propagation (DTP) fails. The key insight is that TP corresponds more closely to Gauss–Newton optimization than to backpropagation, which explains qualitative differences in updates and exposes why DTP struggles when inverses are imperfect. Methodologically, the authors analyze TP formally, identify DTP’s failure mode, and propose a new reconstruction loss plus architectural changes that train feedback weights better and permit direct output-to-hidden feedback; experiments show these fixes improve performance and make forward updates better aligned with true loss gradients.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of test-time adaptation for dense prediction tasks (semantic segmentation and depth estimation), where prior image-level visual prompts obscure spatial details and thus limit domain-specific knowledge extraction. Its key insight is that sparse, pixel-level prompts distributed across the image can preserve spatial context while using only minimal trainable parameters, and that allocating and updating those sparse prompts according to per-pixel distribution shift and per-sample characteristics yields better adaptation. The method, Sparse Visual Domain Prompts (SVDP), places a very small fraction of trainable parameters at selected pixels, with a Domain Prompt Placement (DPP) scheme to allocate parameters to pixels with large domain shift and a Domain Prompt Updating (DPU) strategy that optimizes prompts per target sample during test time. Experiments on standard TTA and continual TTA benchmarks show that SVDP achieves state-of-the-art performance with far fewer tunable parameters.

result.text: The paper addresses scalable, unbiased generative modeling on manifolds, where existing continuous normalizing flow methods either require costly simulation, scale poorly to high dimensions, or rely on biased approximations for essential quantities. The key insight is that by defining a simple, analytically tractable premetric one can construct closed-form target vector fields for flow matching that generalize the Euclidean case to arbitrary geometries, removing the need for divergence computation and simulation on many domains. The method, Riemannian Flow Matching (RFM), uses this premetric to specify target velocity fields and leverages spectral decompositions to efficiently compute the premetric and associated targets on general manifolds (including meshes with curvature and boundaries), enabling simulation-free or tractable training and yielding state-of-the-art results on diverse non-Euclidean datasets.

result.text: The paper addresses the high memory cost of KV caching during generative inference with large language models by proposing a plug-and-play way to compress the KV cache without retraining. The key insight is that attention heads exhibit distinct, predictable structures—some focus on local context, some on special tokens, and some attend broadly—so the cache can be adapted per-head to keep only the vectors that matter. The method profiles attention patterns cheaply, then constructs an adaptive KV cache that evicts long-range entries on local-focused heads, drops non-special tokens on special-token-focused heads, and retains full caches for globally attending heads; this profiling-guided FastGen approach reduces GPU memory use substantially while preserving generation quality and requires no expensive fine-tuning.

result.text: We propose Uncertainty-Adaptive Partial-OT CLIP, which couples in-batch partial optimal transport soft matching with per-sample contrastive temperatures driven by evidential aleatoric uncertainty. Concretely, lightweight prototype-based evidential heads on the image and text encoders estimate sample uncertainty and local density; these signals jointly set each example’s partial-transport mass budget and InfoNCE temperature via learned monotone schedules optimized under a robust objective, so ambiguous or low-density samples transport less mass and are contrasted more softly while confident, reliable samples receive sharper alignment. We further stabilize training with cross-/in-modal geometric consistency regularization and uncertainty-aware hard-negative shaping. This design targets web-scale noise and the modality gap, yielding more interchangeable embeddings, stronger long-tail transfer, and calibrated retrieval confidence.

args.text: We introduce Compositional Energy-Guided Architecture-and-Weight Diffusion (CEAWD), which casts task-conditioned joint generation of architectures and initial weights as score-model sampling under a sum of constraint energies for accuracy proxies, latency, memory, and robustness. Building on EBM-style compositional samplers with Metropolis-corrected updates, we replace heuristic classifier-free guidance with principled energy composition, where accuracy energies come from GenNAS-like self-supervised signals and compute/robustness energies are predicted from computation-aware encodings (CATE) of candidate architectures. We train the joint diffusion on a model zoo with layer-normalized weight latents and dataset conditioning, and evaluate Pareto fronts on NAS-Bench-360 and hardware-specific latency targets, showing improved stability and multi-objective optimality over standard guided diffusion. Ablations isolate contributions of energy terms and acceptance correction, and we demonstrate cross-architecture transfer by sampling compatible weights for unseen architectures.

result.text: Manifold-to-Prototype Self-Paced Cross-Modal Hashing (MaP-SCMH) is a three-stage curriculum for robust cross-modal hashing under noisy correspondences and domain shift. Stage 1 mines intra-modal affinities via bi-directional random walks on modality-specific graphs to obtain graph-consistent pseudo-similarities and trains hash codes with a parameter-free bit-balance layer and a code-memory contrastive objective for stable, high-entropy quantization. Stage 2 aligns the modalities by learning prototype-anchored features on a shared unit hypersphere and supervising quantization so that relations are preserved when mapping to a Hamming hypersphere. Stage 3 activates a complementary-supervision head with momentum-based correspondence correction, whose accepted pairs are scheduled by instance- and feature-level self-paced weights so the model gradually absorbs harder, corrected pairs while filtering noise.

result.text: We introduce Compositional Energy-Guided Architecture-and-Weight Diffusion (CEAWD), which casts task-conditioned joint generation of architectures and initial weights as score-model sampling under a sum of constraint energies for accuracy proxies, latency, memory, and robustness. Building on EBM-style compositional samplers with Metropolis-corrected updates, we replace heuristic classifier-free guidance with principled energy composition, where accuracy energies come from GenNAS-like self-supervised signals and compute/robustness energies are predicted from computation-aware encodings (CATE) of candidate architectures. We train the joint diffusion on a model zoo with layer-normalized weight latents and dataset conditioning, and evaluate Pareto fronts on NAS-Bench-360 and hardware-specific latency targets, showing improved stability and multi-objective optimality over standard guided diffusion. Ablations isolate contributions of energy terms and acceptance correction, and we demonstrate cross-architecture transfer by sampling compatible weights for unseen architectures.

result.text: The paper addresses rigorous optimization guarantees for deep equilibrium models—implicit neural networks whose layers are defined by fixed points—when training non-convex objectives for regression and classification. The key insight is that, despite weight-tied nonlinearity and non-convexity, the gradient flow of these implicit models converges globally and linearly to a global optimum without any overparameterization requirement on width, and that the implicit gradient dynamics emulate a trust-region Newton method for an equivalent shallow explicit model. Methodologically, the authors analyze the continuous-time gradient dynamics using tools tailored to implicit layers and implicit differentiation, proving global linear convergence and deriving a formal connection between implicit-layer dynamics and trust-region Newton updates, supported by numerical observations that motivate further study of implicit bias in such models.

args.text: We propose Hodge-CNF, a manifold continuous normalizing flow that parameterizes the tangent vector field via a Hodge decomposition into exact (gradient), coexact (divergence-free), and harmonic components using discrete exterior calculus on meshes or point clouds. Because only the exact component contributes to log-density change (via the manifold divergence), we can decouple likelihood control from geometry-aware transport: learn a scalar potential to govern density evolution while using divergence-free and harmonic fields to capture topology-induced mixing around cycles without affecting likelihood. Training projects predicted velocities onto Hodge components and matches either target velocity fields (Riemannian flow matching) or target density paths (probability path divergence), implemented via Poisson solves with the Laplace–Beltrami operator and spectral bases for scalability. This yields topology-aware expressiveness, improved numerical stability, and interpretable control of density vs. mixing on general Riemannian manifolds with exact likelihoods.

result.text: We propose Wasserstein Prompt Fields (WPF) for dense continual test-time adaptation in vision–language models, modeling domain shift as a spatially varying, low-parameter prompt field attached to pixels that transports per-pixel features from a source-domain barycenter to the evolving target. Concretely, we build a per-pixel feature bank over multiple source domains and compute a Wasserstein barycenter as a style prior; at test time, we estimate a low-rank optimal transport map from this barycenter to the target using unlabeled images and update only the sparse prompt field under a trust-region constraint. To stabilize adaptation without labels, we employ swapped-prediction consistency between an online and EMA prompt head and a homeostatic gate that blends shared low-rank with plastic high-rank prompt components per region to mitigate forgetting. WPF enables fast, label-free adaptation for segmentation and depth while accommodating target label-proportion shifts via the OT objective.

The key insight is to build a learned surrogate that predicts per-example errors and to actively sample labels to improve that surrogate in a way optimized for accurate global error estimation, rather than treating labeled points as direct Monte Carlo samples. Their method, Active Surrogate Estimators (ASEs), trains an interpolating surrogate model over unlabeled inputs and uses a novel acquisition function called XWED to select which examples to label so as to most reduce estimation error of the target metric. Empirically, ASEs achieve substantially better label-efficiency than prior active testing approaches on challenging deep neural network evaluation tasks.

result.text: We propose a skeleton-conditioned predictive codec for dynamic 3D Gaussian avatars that enables low-bitrate, low-latency telepresence. Gaussians are grouped into bone-anchored clusters whose next-frame position/scale/opacity and view-dependent color are predicted by applying SMPL-X pose transforms together with a lightweight state-space residual model, so the encoder transmits only small residual updates. An anchor-level autoregressive entropy model compresses these residuals and hyper-features, while an EVA-style per-pixel confidence triggers selective intra-frame refresh of uncertain regions (e.g., hands/face), and periodic LightGaussian-style distillation/quantization keeps the representation compact. This pose-aware temporal coding turns static 3DGS compression into a streaming avatar codec that preserves fine details under fast motion at a fraction of current bandwidth and integrates cleanly with existing Gaussian avatar pipelines.

Concretely, the method projects image features to a spherical feature field, applies SO(3)-equivariant convolutions to produce a rotation-dependent score function, and outputs a full distribution over orientations that can be sampled at arbitrary resolution. result.text: The paper addresses how to train Continuous Normalizing Flows (CNFs) when data lie on manifolds, avoiding the computational and conceptual difficulties of matching distributions by solving ODEs for each training step. The key insight is to match the entire probability density path of the CNF to a chosen target path via a novel probability path divergence (PPD), derived from a logarithmic mass conservation relation that yields a linear first-order PDE linking the CNF vector field and the log target densities. The key insight is that this gap arises from two interacting causes: (1) standard neural network initialization biases each encoder’s outputs into a narrow cone so that different encoders start separated, and (2) contrastive optimization—particularly the temperature hyperparameter—preserves or enforces a nonzero separation between modalities during training. result.text: The paper tackles the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff in large vision-language models for long-term, dense video streaming, where many vision tokens improve understanding but blow up memory and computation. The key insight is that instead of reducing the number of vision tokens (which can lose cues for LLMs’ contextual key-value caches), one can learn to skip expensive per-layer computation for a large fraction of tokens—i.e., a mixture-of-depths strategy that routes most vision tokens forward unchanged while only a subset receive full transformer processing. The proposed VideoLLM-MoD trains per-layer gating to bypass computation for ~80% of vision tokens, thereby cutting overall training time and memory (≈42% time, ≈30% memory) while preserving or improving downstream performance. result.text: Certified Prototype-Smoothed Cross-Modal Hashing (Cert-PSCMH) provides retrieval guarantees under both input perturbations and bit flips by jointly smoothing in feature and Hamming spaces. args.text: Spectral Control Propagation (SCP): a local, single-phase learning rule for deep equilibrium and recurrent systems that unifies least-control training with holomorphic equilibrium propagation. We inject small sinusoidal control signals at outputs (and optionally intermediate controllers), and each synapse performs lock-in demodulation of activity correlations at prescribed frequencies to extract first-harmonic sensitivities, yielding exact gradient estimates at finite amplitudes while updating weights to minimize time-averaged control effort under the equilibrium constraint. The key insight is to apply an anchor-level autoregressive context model—grouping anchors into multiple levels so that uncoded anchors can be predicted from already coded anchors in coarser levels—to exploit inter-anchor dependencies and improve entropy modeling.
