args.text: Fourier-Control Propagation (FCP) for implicit equilibrium networks: combine least-control learning with holomorphic, finite-amplitude teaching signals to obtain single-phase, local credit assignment robust to noise. At each training step, we inject small complex sinusoidal control currents that steer the network toward targets; the first Fourier coefficients of state and control around the fixed point provide Jacobian-vector products that, when used in a control-minimization objective, yield Gauss-Newton/trust-region-like updates for the implicit model. This recovers DEQ-style second-order descent with no stored activations, no weight transport, and locally computable updates, unifying DFC-style control learning with EP’s oscillatory gradient readout for EBMs while extending to general implicit dynamics. Because signals are oscillatory and local, the method is naturally compatible with noisy analog or neuromorphic substrates.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of learning generative models on complex manifolds (e.g., spheres, tori, implicit surfaces) where existing Euclidean flow methods are either geometry-restricted or computationally costly. The key insight is to parameterize the model density directly as a source (prior) density minus the divergence of a neural network, because divergence is a local linear differential operator that is straightforward to compute on manifolds and sidesteps costly ODE-based change-of-variable computations. The resulting Moser Flow is a continuous normalizing flow whose training does not require backpropagation through an ODE solver, yields an explicit density representation that improves fidelity, and is provably a universal density approximator under mild assumptions. Empirically, Moser Flow enables the first effective flow-based sampling on general curved surfaces and outperforms existing CNFs in density estimation, sample quality, and training efficiency on synthetic and real-world geoscience benchmarks.

result.text: We propose Reliability-Calibrated Compositional Guidance for joint architecture-and-weight diffusion, which dynamically reweights multiple proxy energies by their estimated task-specific trust to steer generation toward robust, high-performing, resource-feasible models. result.text: The paper tackles the storage and runtime inefficiency of point-based real-time neural rendering—specifically the large, gigabyte-scale collections of 3D Gaussians produced by SfM that impede scalability and splatting speed. Its key insight is that most Gaussians contribute little to global scene reconstruction and can therefore be identified and compacted without perceptible quality loss by borrowing ideas from network pruning and distillation. The method, LightGaussian, ranks Gaussians by a computed global significance, prunes and recovers low-significance elements, distills higher-degree spherical harmonic coefficients into lower-degree ones using pseudo-view augmentation, and applies significance-aware vector quantization to reduce bitwidth; this pipeline yields about 15× compression and large FPS gains while preserving visual fidelity and generalizes to other Gaussian-based 3D representations.

args.text: Frequency-Control Propagation (FCP) unifies least-control learning with finite-amplitude, holomorphic equilibrium propagation to train implicit/equilibrium networks using only local signals. We inject sinusoidal control fields at distinct carrier frequencies to outputs and intermediate modules, then demodulate the first harmonic of each unit’s activity to obtain exact local gradient estimates while simultaneously minimizing control energy; the resulting rule trains forward and feedback pathways in one continuous phase and tolerates strong, noisy feedback. For DEQ-style implicit layers, these demodulated updates approximate trust-region Newton steps without explicit Jacobians, yielding faster, more stable convergence than standard EP/DFA under neuromorphic noise budgets. We hypothesize FCP recovers DFC/EP in limiting cases and propose benchmarks on ImageNet-32 and meta-learning tasks with ablations over frequency-division multiplexing, control budgets, and hardware noise.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of building flexible, general-purpose normalizing flows that respect non‑Euclidean data geometry without requiring handcrafted, manifold‑specific layers. Its key insight is that Neural ODEs can be generalized to arbitrary manifolds using only local geometric information, enabling continuous-time flows whose dynamics remain on the manifold and whose probability densities can be tracked via a continuous change-of-variables formula. The authors introduce Neural Manifold ODEs and use them to construct Manifold Continuous Normalizing Flows (MCNFs), which integrate vector fields defined in local charts (or via embeddings) to transport probability mass while computing log-densities through an ODE for the instantaneous change of variables. Empirically, MCNFs are simple to apply across different manifolds and produce improved density estimation and downstream task performance compared with prior manifold-specific flow designs.

args.text: I propose Holo-Control Propagation (HCP), a single-phase, biologically plausible learning rule for equilibrium and other implicit networks that unifies least-control optimal-control training with holomorphic equilibrium propagation’s finite-signal gradient readout. HCP injects a small complex sinusoidal control at the outputs and performs strictly local Hebbian updates proportional to the first-harmonic of pre–post activity to minimize control energy, yielding exact gradients under holomorphic dynamics and Gauss–Newton-like updates more generally via equilibrium sensitivity. For deep equilibrium models, the induced update aligns with a trust-region/Newton direction and remains robust under strong, noisy feedback, while avoiding storage of intermediate states. We will benchmark HCP on DEQs, recurrent/meta-learning tasks, and neuromorphic substrates, ablating control amplitude, noise, and frequency against backprop, DFC, and EP.

The key insight is that the variational lower bound for continuous-time diffusion on a manifold can be formulated so that maximizing it is equivalent to Riemannian score matching, and that evaluating model likelihoods requires computing a Riemannian divergence term that can be handled efficiently. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of generative modeling for data concentrated on low-dimensional manifolds embedded in high-dimensional ambient spaces, where standard density estimators struggle to capture manifold geometry and yield poor inference. The key insight is to decouple learning the manifold geometry from learning a tractable probability density on that manifold, enabling models that represent both the support and the distribution on it more faithfully than ambient-space flows. The authors introduce manifold-learning flows (M-flows), which combine invertible coordinate maps (like normalizing flows) to parametrize a learned manifold with a separate density model on the manifold and a training algorithm that alternates or separates manifold and density updates rather than relying solely on maximum likelihood. Experiments show M-flows can recover manifold structure, improve dimensionality reduction and denoising, and yield better inference and out-of-distribution detection than standard flows operating in the ambient space.

result.text: The paper addresses limitations of randomized smoothing for certifiable robustness beyond the standard isotropic Gaussian case, focusing on how the certified ℓ_p radius scales with input dimension d. The key insight is that for a broad class of i.i.d. smoothing distributions the maximum certifiable ℓ_p radius necessarily shrinks with dimension — for p>2 it decays as O(1/d^{1/2-1/p}) and for many natural non-Gaussian smoothers the decay is even worse — so Gaussian smoothing is essentially optimal (up to constants) for p≥2. The authors prove lower bounds on the achievable certified radius for i.i.d. and generalized Gaussian smoothers and complementary upper bounds for other distributions (e.g., uniform in ℓ_1 or ℓ_∞ balls), and validate these theoretical scaling laws with CIFAR experiments, demonstrating a fundamental “curse of dimensionality” for smoothing-based certification in high dimensions.
